note:
The “thirtieth” year is most likely Ezekiel’s age at the time of his prophetic call. A trainee for the priesthood ordinarily assumes the full responsibilities of the office at age thirty (Num. 4:3). Instead of achieving this important goal, Ezekiel is living in exile far from the temple in Jerusalem and is unable to fulfill his calling. As a priest, Ezekiel is responsible to teach the law of God to the people, explaining its implications and helping them “distinguish between clean and unclean” (Ezek. 22:26; cf. Deut. 33:10). As a prophet, he delivers God’s words of blessing and curse to the people, depending on their faithfulness to their covenant obligations. Additionally, prophets normally intercede with God for the people. Ezek­iel’s ministry includes aspects of both priestly and prophetic mediation between God and the Jewish people in Babylon.

**exiles.** Due to the close connection between gods and particular lands in the ancient world, those exiled from Judah likely feel abandoned by the Lord in Babylon. Ezekiel is called to serve as a prophet to his fellow exiles in Babylon as a sign that the Lord has not forgotten them. On the contrary, the Lord will be a sanctuary for them there (11:16).

verse_quote: the fifth year of the exile of King Jehoiachin.
note: July 593 B.C. Most of the dates in the book of Ezekiel are calculated from Jehoiachin’s exile, which took place in 597 B.C. (see 2 Kin. 24:10–13; Ezek. 40:1). This means that Ezekiel’s prophecy begins during the period when Jehoiachin’s uncle, Zedekiah, is ruling Judah as a semiautonomous vassal kingdom of Babylon. Four years after Ezek­iel’s prophetic ministry begins, Zedekiah rebels unsuccessfully against Nebuchadnezzar. As a result of this rebellion, the Babylonians destroy the city of Jerusalem and burn its temple in 586 B.C. The arrival of the news of Jerusalem’s destruction among the exiles in ch. 24 is a turning point in the prophet’s ministry, as Ezekiel shifts his focus from the certainty of further judgment on those who have remained in Judah to the proclamation of a future hope for the remnant of God’s people. From the outset, Ezekiel views Zedekiah as a mere stand-in for the lawful king of Judah, Jehoiachin.

Jews living outside their homeland commonly establish places of worship along streams of water (Ps. 137:1; Acts 16:13). Two cuneiform texts from Nippur mention a _narukabari_(“Great River”) that is probably the Chebar, which is a large irrigation canal that brings water from the Euphrates below Babylon. Babylonian practice is to resettle conquered peoples in homogeneous groups, allowing them to retain their ethnic identity, unlike the Assyrians, whose mode of operation was to disperse and scatter the populations that they exiled. This difference allows the exiles in Babylon to form a distinct community and return to their homeland as a cohesive group after seventy years in exile. Such a return was not possible for those exiled from the northern kingdom by the Assyrians in 722 B.C.

Ezekiel’s inaugural vision should be compared with the call narratives of Moses (Ex. 3), Isaiah (Is. 6), and Jeremiah (Jer. 1). Like Moses, the model prophet (Deut. 18:15, 18), later prophets ordinarily begin their prophetic careers by being admitted into the divine presence. In the heavenly council, they hear the words of God. The prophets report such experiences not so much as autobiography but because their admission to the divine council is the basis for their claim to prophetic authority. It is one of the qualifications that distinguish the true prophet from the false (1 Kin. 22:19–28; Jer. 23:16–18).

**1:4 stormy wind.** For whirlwind and storm as a mode of theophany (a manifestation or appearance of God), see 2 Kin. 2:1, 11; Job 38:1; 40:6; Pss. 77:18; 83:15; 148:8; Is. 29:6; 66:15; Jer. 4:13; 23:19; 30:23; Nah. 1:3; Zech. 9:14. In this case, the storm is coming from the north, the direction from which Israel’s enemies often came. This suggests that the true enemy Judah has to fear is not Babylon but the Lord Himself (cf. Jer. 1:13, 14).

Describes the first appearance of the famous “living creatures” in the book of Ezekiel. When these creatures appear again in ch. 10, they are identified as “cherubim” (10:1, 15, 16, 20), angelic creatures who form the Lord’s bodyguard around the ark in the Most Holy Place (1 Kin. 6:27; 2 Chr. 3:11, 12). Similar creatures are present in John’s vision of the divine throne (Rev. 4:6–9). They have wings as well as legs, enabling them to run or fly equally swiftly, making it impossible to escape from them.

The four faces of the creatures represent four realms of creation. Man is supreme and faces outward. The ox is the head of domestic animals; the lion is the head of wild animals; and the eagle is the head of birds. Since each has four faces, they can look in all four directions (north, south, east, west) at once, making it impossible to hide from their all-seeing gaze.

Fire is a regular component of theophanies in the OT (Gen. 15:17; Ex. 3:2; 13:21, 22; 14:24; 19:18; 24:17; Num. 11:1; Deut. 1:33; 4:11, 12, 24, 33, 36; 5:22–26; 9:3; Pss. 18:8; 78:14, 21). It represents God’s power to judge (e.g., Gen. 19:24; Ezek. 10:2)., 14

The cherubim are pulling the divine war chariot. It can move equally easily in any direction because each wheel has another intersecting it at right angles (“a wheel within a wheel,” v.17). Each wheel is full of eyes. These themes highlight the threatening aspect of the Lord’s appearing: when He comes for judgment, there is nowhere to run and nowhere to hide.

The expanse serves as a divider between the realms of earth and heaven, like the sky (see Gen. 1:6). This reference, along with references to living creatures, cherubim, and a rainbow, recalls the opening chapters of Genesis. Just as God once destroyed the original world He had made through a devastating flood and restored it through Noah (Gen. 6–9), Ezekiel’s world is being unmade so that it can ultimately be restored.

Below the expanse, the living creatures make a distinctive and terrifyingly loud sound as they fly. This sound often accompanies theophanies that involve the divine army (2 Sam. 5:24; 2 Kin. 7:6; Is. 13:4; 66:6; Joel 2:5; cf. Gen. 3:8; Ex. 19:19; Is. 6:4). See particularly 3:12, 13; 10:5.

Above the expanse is a throne with someone resembling a human being on it. Here, as elsewhere in the vision, Ezekiel seems almost at a loss for words to describe what he sees. The light radiating from the divine presence is overwhelming (Dan. 7:9), for God dwells “in unapproachable light” (1 Tim. 6:16). Yet as in Dan. 7 and Rev. 1, the divine figure who comes to judge the world appears in human form. In the fullness of time, the Ancient of Days will take on flesh and become the Son of Man, Jesus Christ. The day of God’s appearing is terrifying, yet for His people it is comforting to know that the One who sits on the throne has been made like us in every way, except without sin (Heb. 4:15)., 27

verse_quote: the bow that is in the cloud.
note:
The image of a rainbow among storm clouds reflects the prospect of judgment tempered with mercy. The storm clouds threaten imminent destruction, but the rainbow recalls God’s promise to Noah (Gen. 9:16, 17). Although the coming Babylonian invasion will destroy many of the people, God will not forget His promise to preserve a remnant.

**I fell on my face.** In light of this vision of awesome and inescapable judgment, the prophet falls down as though dead. The primary warning of the passage is not for him or his fellow exiles, but for those who have remained in Judah and Jerusalem. He is called to bring a message of hope to those in exile. The same glorious God who threatens comprehensive judgment can also build up what He has torn down (cf. Jer. 1:10).

As in other call narratives, after the prophet comes into the divine presence, God announces the commission, normally with a statement that He is sending that person (2:3; Ex. 3:10; Judg. 6:14; Is. 6:8; Jer. 1:7).

**2:1 Son of man.** Or “Son of Adam.” God addresses Ezekiel this way more than ninety times in this book. The phrase emphasizes the prophet’s humanity and frailty, especially as it stands in such proximity to a vision of God’s glory and the heavenly beings that surround Him. It also distinguishes him from his contemporaries, whom the Lord calls “the people (lit. ‘sons’) of Israel.” They are a “nation of rebels,” the true heirs of their ancestor, Jacob/Israel, whose distinguishing feature was struggling with God (Gen. 32:28). As “Son of Adam,” Ezekiel represents the first member of a new community of faith, indwelt by the Spirit and empowered for a life of new obedience (2:2). As happens with the dry bones of ch. 37, when the Spirit comes into the prophet, Ezekiel stands on his feet obediently ready to serve (cf. 37:10). In this way, he personally foreshadows the salvation that he declares to his fellow exiles.

Jesus is the true Son of Man, combining in one person the glories of the heavenly Son of Man depicted in Dan. 7:13, 14 with the “mere humanity” that is the more common import of the phrase. In His earthly ministry, Jesus became like us in our humanity, sharing our weaknesses and sorrows, yet without sin (Mark 10:45; 1 Pet. 2:22). Indwelt by the Spirit, He obeyed and became the last Adam, the founding member of God’s new community of faith (1 Cor. 15). As such, in His resurrection Jesus is the down payment on the new community of Spirit-transformed sons of Adam and daughters of Eve who find their hope in Him.

These metaphors refer to those who are going to persecute Ezekiel for bringing an unpopular message from God (1 Kin. 18:4; Jer. 20:7–18; Matt. 23:29–31, 34, 37). His ministry will be painful and frustrating and his audience unresponsive (cf. Is. 6:9–13). However, Ezekiel is not responsible for the people’s rejection of his message; his task is to deliver it faithfully, so that when God holds them to account, they will not be able to deny that a prophet has been among them.

In other accounts of the prophetic call, once the commission is given, God often provides a sign to confirm it (Ex. 3:12; Jer. 1:11–14). Moses said that God would put His word into the mouths of the prophets (Deut. 18:18). Here that promise is depicted visibly, as Ezekiel has to eat a scroll covered with unappetizing words of God’s judgment. Yet Ezekiel is not like his contemporaries who refuse to obey God. Surprisingly, although the scroll looks distasteful, when Ezekiel eats it, he finds it as sweet as honey. Obedience turns a bitter meal into pleasant fare, while disobedience ruins even the best food.

Scrolls in Ezekiel’s day are ordinarily written only on one side, but here the indictment against the people’s sin is too long to be contained on one side of the scroll, and it spills over to fill the other side as well (cf. Zech. 5:3; Rev. 5:1).

**lamentation and mourning and woe.** Most of the first half of the book of Ezekiel consists of oracles of judgment against Judah (chs. 1–24).

Ezekiel is sent to the Lord’s own people, but they do not receive him (cf. John 1:11). If the prophet were to be sent to a people who speak a different language and have a different culture, it would be far easier to reach them with God’s message.

The Lord identifies His messengers with Himself (cf. Luke 10:16; John 13:20). The house of Israel is not only closed to listening to Ezekiel but is also closed to hearing the One who has sent the prophet to them.
Ezekiel’s name in Hebrew means “God makes strong, hardens.”

Ezekiel more than once describes his visionary experiences in terms of transport by the Spirit (v. 14; 8:3; 11:1, 24; 40:1–3; 43:5). See 2 Kin. 2:11, 16; 2 Cor. 12:1, 2. Here, the Spirit brings him back from his vision to the ordinary world of the exiles.

As the prophetic spokesman for God, he begins to feel some of the bitterness and anger that God feels against sin. At the same time, as one of the exiles, Ezekiel is overwhelmed at the prospect of such a fearsome judgment to come. Like Job’s counselors, he sits silently for seven days (Job 2:13), unable to say a word in the face of such deep tragedy.

**Tel-abib.** The precise location is not known., 15
This phrase occurs more than fifty times in Ezekiel, more than in any other prophetic book.

Ezekiel is responsible for those to whom he ministers and has to warn them of any impending threat, just as a watchman for a city acts as a lookout, providing advance warning of an enemy’s approach. Failure to issue the warning would make him accountable for any misfortune that resulted. The image of a watchman also occurs elsewhere in the OT (33:1–9; cf. Is. 56:10; Jer. 6:17; Hos. 9:8). People in a city never ignore the cry of an ordinary watchman, yet they will not listen to Ezekiel (vv. 6, 7; cf. Is. 22:1–14). In this case, the approaching enemy is God Himself.

The prophet is to preach equally to all, and the individual’s true status as righteous or wicked will be revealed by their response to his message. Whether they were previously regarded as “righteous” or “wicked,” if they heed his words, they will receive life, while they will die if they ignore him. The distinguishing characteristic that leads to life rather than death is thus not previous status but present faith in the Lord’s word through His prophet.
Ezekiel uses this phrase to describe how revelation comes to him (v. 14; 8:1; 33:22; 37:1; 40:1).

The word means an open area between mountains and can be translated either “valley” or “plain.” The same term occurs in Ezekiel’s vision of the “valley” of dry bones (37:1). There, again, he falls on his face when he sees the glory of the Lord. Seeing God’s glory is not something to which someone becomes accustomed; it is always overwhelming.

The prophet is God’s prisoner, shut up in his own house and tied up with cords. Even his tongue is under house arrest, as it were, so that he becomes unable to speak. The prophet is not completely mute, but speaks only when he receives revelation from God. Ezekiel delivers many oracles to the exiles in the six years between his call and the destruction of Jerusalem. However, he is not permitted to intercede for them with God because the time for dialogue between God and His people has passed. Ezekiel remains speechless until news of Jerusalem’s fall arrives in Babylon (24:27). At that point, with the completion of God’s judgment on His people, the prophet is free to speak on their behalf once more.

Prophets sometimes perform sign-acts that illustrate their messages. This is especially the case when they are preaching to an unresponsive audience (1 Kin. 11:30; 22:11; 2 Kin. 13:17; Is. 20:2–4; Jer. 13:1–14; 19:1–10). Bricks or clay tablets, about ten inches (25 cm) by twenty inches (51 cm) in size, have been found throughout Mesopotamia with maps or architectural drawings inscribed on them. The prophet uses a clay tablet with a picture of Jerusalem as the centerpiece of a tableau depicting the siege of the city in 586 B.C., which ended with its destruction.

The prophet uses a large flat griddle on which bread is baked in an oven. Since the prophet represents God in this miniature drama, the iron griddle standing on edge represents the wall that exists between God and Jerusalem. Their prayers will not reach Him, and He will not intervene on their behalf. In fact, Ezekiel depicts God with His face aggressively directed toward the city.

The dual nature of the prophetic office—representing God to the people and the people to God—is seen in the second half of the symbolic action. Having represented God in the first part, the prophet now represents the people and bears their sin (cf. Ex. 32:30–32; Rom. 9:3).

The time period to which the numbers 390 and forty refer is hard to interpret. Each day represents one year (v. 6; cf. Num. 14:34; Dan. 9:24–27). It may be that the forty days do not follow the 390 days (for a total of 430), but are concurrent with them. A 390-year history of sin would stretch back almost to the building of Solomon’s temple. The forty years for the house of Judah may represent a lost generation, like the generation that bore the wrath of God for forty years in the wilderness (Num. 14:34). On the other hand, some regard the total of 430 years as a symbolic reference to the length of Israel’s sojourn in Egypt (Ex. 12:40, 41). This hints at the possibility of a new exodus for God’s people at the end of this time period. Jewish interpretation assumes that the number represents the years up until the reign of Josiah; however, his reign is not included since he is considered righteous., 6

verse_quote: set your face toward the siege of Jerusalem.
note: Ezekiel was to take both parts in the drama, representing God in His anger against the city as well as the city itself.

Lying on his side while bound probably means that Ezekiel is immobile for a significant part of each day. Yet it is unlikely that he is permanently bound since he still has to prepare his meals (vv. 8–13).

Ezekiel must exist on siege rations while he enacts the siege of Jerusalem. These rations reflect the privations during a siege (Deut. 28:52–57; 2 Kin. 6:25; 7:12; Jer. 15:2; 19:9), when there is not enough of any one kind of grain to make a whole loaf. As a result, Ezekiel’s food is a strange and unpalatable mixture of grains and legumes.
About eight ounces (0.24 L ; text note).

verse_quote: the sixth part of a hin.
note: This water ration is just over a pint (0.6 L).

Ceremonial cleanness is all but impossible to observe during a siege, even for a priest like Ezek­iel. It is even harder in exile. Human excrement is considered impure in the Mosaic law (Deut. 23:13), and the prophet is repulsed by God’s command to him, protesting that he has never violated the dietary laws restricting the kinds of food Israel is permitted to eat (44:31; cf. Ex. 22:31; Lev. 7:19–24; 11:8, 39, 40; 22:8; Deut. 14:3, 8). God permits him to substitute cattle manure, which is a widely used fuel in parts of the Near East in our own day.

Cutting facial hair was a matter of great personal shame in the ancient Near East (2 Sam. 10:4, 5; Is. 7:20; 50:6), as it represented a symbolic loss of manhood. Like the Assyrians before them, the Babylonians used it as a means of humiliating captured soldiers. Using a sharp sword as a razor connects this sign-act with the preceding ones and points to the arrival of the time of judgment. The careful weighing and dividing of the hair suggests God’s carefully measured judgment on His people.

Ezekiel interprets the symbolism of vv. 1–4: the hairs burned in fire represent those who will die of plague or disease during the siege; the hairs struck with the sword represent those who will die in battle and the aftermath of the siege; the hairs dispersed by the wind represent those who will be carried into exile. Ezekiel does not elaborate on the significance of the few hairs that are retained in the folds of his garment, but they symbolize the survivors who will remain in Jerusalem (Jer. 40:7–12). Some of this tiny group will subsequently be removed and destroyed by fire. Very few of those in Jerusalem will survive the wrath to come.

Israel’s idolatry and refusal to obey the Lord’s commands will have serious consequences (see Lev. 26:1, 2, 14, 15). As a result, the curses threatened in the rest of Lev. 26 will fall on them. These include cannibalism (Lev. 26:29), being scattered among the nations (Lev. 26:33), famine (26:26) and disease, and the sword (26:25). Yet God promises in Lev. 26:44, 45 that these covenant curses will not be His final word. He will remember His covenant and spare a remnant of His people in spite of their sin and unfaithfulness.

Ezekiel’s address to the mountains of Israel as if he can see them has prompted some to suggest that for part of his ministry Ezekiel is in Israel instead of with the exiles in Babylon. However, though the hills and mountains of Israel are his metaphorical audience, the real audience is the community of exiles. Compare Ezekiel’s prophecy regarding the people of Edom, which is addressed to Mount Seir (ch. 35). This part of Israel is the nation’s political heartland, but it has likewise become infected with idolatry, marked by many pagan places of worship.

The Canaanites normally worshiped their gods on hilltops. God commanded the Israelites to eradicate the high places when they came into the land (Num. 33:52; Deut. 12:1–3; 33:29). However, the high places have continued to flourish long after the temple was built (16:16; Jer. 7:31; 19:5; 32:35; 48:35). The people have been worshiping Canaanite gods there or have converted the pagan shrines for use in a combination of Canaanite practices and their own. The continued existence of the high places is a particular offense to the writer of the book of Kings (1 Kin. 11:7; 12:31, 32; 13:2, 32; 14:23; 2 Kin. 12:3; 14:4; 15:4, 35; 17:29; 23:5, 8, 13, 15, 19, 20).
The shrines will be desecrated by the presence of dead bodies (9:7; cf. Num. 19:16, 18; 1 Kin. 13:2; 2 Kin. 23:14–16; 2 Chr. 23:14, 15; 34:5).

verse_quote: you shall know that I am the Lord.
note: Ezekiel makes frequent use of this “recognition formula” (cf. 7:4, 9; 11:10, 12; 12:20). The Lord reveals Himself as the ruler of history by announcing events beforehand. He will demonstrate his power by bringing judgment upon His rebellious people, just as the terms of the covenant at Mount Sinai require.

Ezekiel introduces the remnant theme (9:8; 11:12, 13; 12:16; 14:22, 23; 20:39–44). The remnant is a group or individual who has experienced some calamity, ordinarily in judgment for sin, and has survived. This group of survivors becomes the nucleus for the continuation of the group; they embody the future hopes of the people, and they inherit the promises of God afresh. The exile is to be a period of purging and refining so that a purified people can emerge from it.

See text note. The exact location is uncertain, although the context seems to require a well-known place. The Hebrew letters for “d” and “r” look similar and were occasionally confused by scribes. Nebuchadnezzar set up his court at Riblah and there executed many of Jerusalem’s military and civilian leaders after its fall (2 Kin. 25:6, 21). The Lord can demonstrate His power and holiness by destroying rebels as well as by purifying them.

The judgment spreads outward from Jerusalem to the mountains of Israel, and then to the four corners of the land.

**the end is upon you.** Judgment is no longer merely nigh, as was the case in the previous oracles, but is actually upon them. There is no chance of God’s changing His mind or relenting, for the people’s judgment is richly deserved for their sins.

OT prophets often speak of “the day” or “the day of the Lord” (30:3–9; cf. Is. 2:12–17; 13:6–10; 34:8–12; 61:1–3; 63:3–6; Joel 2; 3; Amos 5:18–20; Obad. 8, 15; Zeph. 1:1, 2:15; Zech. 14; Mal. 4:1–3). This is the day when the Lord comes to judge His enemies and to vindicate His name. Depending on the context in which it is spoken by the prophet, the day of the Lord can mean joy or sorrow for Israel. For the use of “the day of the Lord” in the NT, see Rom. 2:16; 1 Cor. 1:8; 5:5; 2 Cor. 1:14; Phil. 1:6, 10; 2:16; 2 Tim. 1:12, 18; 4:8; Heb. 10:25; 2 Pet. 2:9; 3:12; Rev. 16:14.

verse_quote: I am the Lord, who strikes.
note: The same God who was once “the Lord, your healer” (Ex. 15:26) has become “the Lord, who strikes.”
Judah’s sin has reached full measure and she is ripe for destruction.

Judah’s end is depicted in two parallel panels, vv. 12–18 and vv. 19–27. Each proclaims the futility of money in the face of imminent conflict, then announces the coming of war and its associated horrors before declaring that all power and strength will be worthless on that day. Whether a buyer or a seller, or even someone with stores of silver and gold, which are the traditional last resort in a crisis, everyone will be forced to dispose of all of their assets. In fact, their silver and gold will not merely be worthless but unclean (v. 20), something hateful and disgusting because of their association with their former idols.

Because the Lord chose Jerusalem as His dwelling and miraculously fought on the city’s behalf in the past (2 Kin. 18; 19; 2 Chr. 32; Is. 36; 37), Judah has long trusted in the notion that the city is inviolable. Ezekiel’s contemporary Jeremiah also warns the inhabitants of the city not to trust in the existence of the temple as a guarantee of their own security (Jer. 7:1–15; 26:1–19).

The prophet sees four different types of idolatry flourishing in the city: (1) worship of the “image of jealousy” (vv. 5, 6); (2) worship of “beasts” (vv. 7–13); (3) the “Tammuz” cult (vv. 14, 15); and (4) worship of the “sun” (v. 16). All segments of society are involved: elders (vv. 11, 12), women (v. 14), and priests (v. 16). The abominations increase in each scene as one approaches the center of Jerusalem, where the temple of the Lord is.

**8:1 In the sixth year, in the sixth month, on the fifth day of the month.** Fourteen months after the initial vision. Much of the time in between was occupied by the sign-acts of ch. 4.

It is not necessary to conclude that Ezekiel goes physically to Jerusalem. His visionary experience of transport is not unlike other visionary experiences in the Bible (3:12, 14; 37:1; 40:1; cf. 2 Cor. 12:2). Judah’s elders gather in the prophet’s house in Babylon, most likely seeking words of encouragement and comfort. Instead, they hear words of condemnation of their sins and those of their community.

**gateway ... north.** This leads from the outer to the inner court of the temple. The north is the direction from which Judah’s enemies normally come, so the idol has likely been placed there in an attempt to guard the temple and city from attack.

Verse 3 defines the image as something that “provokes to jealousy,” that is, it provokes the anger of the God who is jealous for His own honor (Ex. 20:5). God’s glory belongs there (v. 4); the idol does not. This idol is probably an image of Asherah, a Canaanite goddess who is possibly viewed as Yahweh’s consort by the people. Manasseh put an image of this kind in the temple (2 Kin. 21:7).

The first abomination was very public, while the second is very private, behind an entrance concealed by a wall. Seventy elders of Israel, the same number who saw God in Moses’s day (Ex. 24:1–11), are offering incense to animal-shaped deities, an Egyptian practice. The incense is believed to ward off demonic spirits. Instead of seeing God, like the elders of Moses’s day, these elders affirm that “the Lord does not see us.” However, the fact that the Lord gives this vision to His prophet is proof that they are wrong.
Shaphan was a key leader in Josiah’s reform (2 Kin. 22:3–14; 2 Chr. 34:8, 15–20).

At the time of Ezekiel, Tammuz (the Babylonian god Dumuzi) is worshiped both as a fertility god and as the lord of the underworld. Rites used in worship of Tammuz are tied to the annual cycles of death and rebirth of vegetation. When plants wither under the heat of the summer sun, Tammuz is thought to have died and descended to the underworld; mourning rites mark his passing. The reappearance of vegetation is viewed as the return of Tammuz; fertility rites seek to ensure the productivity of the land. Ritual lamentation for a dead idol has now been substituted for the worship of the true and living God.

The area between the altar and the portico of the temple is ordinarily restricted to priests, yet all of the normal rules of the temple are being flouted in this vision. It is likely, therefore, that these are the elders who are the first to be judged in the next chapter (9:6). The temple faces east, yet these men literally turn their backs on the house of God and worship the rising sun instead (2 Kin. 21:5; 23:11). Astral cults were common in the ancient Near East.

The sins denounced in this chapter primarily refer to a comprehensive range of corrupt religious practices. However, corrupt religion is inevitably accompanied by corrupt relations between people, so that the entire land is described as full of violence or lawlessness. This theme is further developed in 9:9 and 11:6. In light of these abominations, judgment on Jerusalem is inevitable.

**branch to their nose.** A defiant and perhaps vulgar gesture.

The nation’s idolatry will not go unpunished (cf. 2 Chr. 15:12, 13). Though the slayers are described as men (vv. 1, 2), they are probably angelic warriors (Ex. 12:23–30; 1 Chr. 21:15–20) who have been assigned to execute the idolaters.

Linen garments are holy and are therefore worn by angels and those in the presence of God (Dan. 10:5; 12:6, 7; Rev. 15:6; 19:8, 14), as well as by priests (Ex. 28:31–42).

**a writing case.** This man is a scribe, apparently charged with keeping the heavenly record (Ex. 32:32, 33; Pss. 69:28; 139:16; Dan. 12:1; Phil. 4:3; Rev. 3:5; 13:8; 17:8; 20:12, 15; 21:27). In this case, the record involves marking out those who are faithful to God in the midst of the general unfaithfulness around them (cf. Mal. 3:16).

**bronze altar.** This altar in the outer courtyard is where the sacrifices are offered.

verse_quote: the glory of the God of Israel.
note: During the old covenant period, the glory cloud that represents the divine presence normally dwells between the cherubim on top of the ark of the covenant. Now it has left the Most Holy Place and moved to the entrance to the temple as the first stage in God’s forsaking Jerusalem (10:18, 19; 11:22, 23).

Before the six destroying angels are unleashed, the Lord sends the priestly figure to mark all those who mourn over the abominations taking place in Jerusalem (cf. Rev. 7:3; 14:9). Those who are marked out in this way will be protected in the destruction of Jerusalem, just as their forefathers in Egypt were protected by the blood of the Passover lamb (Ex. 12:21–23).

As in the first Passover, all who are unprotected will be destroyed, including women and children. No one will escape except those marked on their foreheads. This foreshadows the final day of the Lord, when judgment on those who remain outside of Christ will be similarly all-encompassing. Judgment begins with the house of the Lord (1 Pet. 4:17), starting with the sun-worshipers who were involved in the climactic abomination in ch. 8., 6

Normally, ancient people are careful not to defile the sacred ground of a temple by allowing people to be executed there. Queen Athaliah, for example, was dragged outside the temple before she was put to death (2 Kin. 11:15, 16). In this case, however, the temple has already become so defiled by the sins of the people that the Lord Himself gives the command, “Defile the house.” Once the Lord’s presence has departed, the temple is an empty shell.

Ezekiel fears that the recording angel might not have found anyone faithful to mark and that he will be the sole remnant. In response, the Lord points Ezekiel to the enormity of Israel’s sins, which underscore his fears. Yet at this crucial moment, the recording angel returns and reports that his mission has been a success. Ezekiel is not told how many people have been marked out for salvation, but the angel’s positive report tempers the scope of the judgment.

The indictments in ch. 8 concentrated on idolatry and cultic offenses; here the issue is not the relationship between God and His people, but relations among the people. The prophet is elaborating on the violence and lawlessness mentioned in 8:17.

See note on 1:5–9. The vision of chs. 8–11 is closely connected with the opening vision of ch. 1. Via an expanse, the same heavenly throne-chariot is separated from the creatures that bear it. The whirling wheels are still in motion. However, in this new location of the temple, Ezek­iel is able to recognize that the living creatures of ch. 1 are actually cherubim, the enforcers of divine judgment.

verse_quote: Fill your hands with burning coals.
note: Like Sodom and Gomorrah, the defiled city of Jerusalem will be burned with fire from on high (see Gen. 19). This visionary scene reveals the heavenly acts that precede the historical events in which King Nebuchadnezzar fills the city with corpses and burns it with fire.
The cherub reaches inside the pillar of fire to retrieve the flames that will devour the city (v. 2).

See Deut. 11:12; 2 Chr. 16:9; Prov. 15:3; Zech. 3:9; 4:10; Rev. 4:8. Once again, this reveals the folly of the elders’ statement, “The Lord does not see us” (Ezek. 8:12). He did not previously forsake the land, but now He will, having been driven out by their sin.
This face was an ox or bull in the earlier vision (1:10).

verse_quote: the glory of the Lord went out . . . the east gate.
note: God’s glory departs in stages, slowly, as if reluctant to leave His former home. It departs to the east, the same direction from which it will return in ch. 43., 19

Having seen the divine perspective on Jerusalem, the Spirit enables Ezek­iel to overhear the words of the earthly inhabi­tants.

**Jaazaniah the son of Azzur.** Not the same person as Jaazaniah the son of Shaphan (8:11).

verse_quote: The time is not near to build houses.
note:
The counsel given by the twenty-five prominent men is not entirely clear, but it is likely that they are asking a rhetorical question: “Isn’t it time to build houses?” If so, they are advising the people that Jerusalem’s future is secure enough to invest in building houses, which is not merely foolish advice but wicked counsel in this context, since it assumes that God cannot or will not act against the sins all around them.

**cauldron ... meat.** Jerusalem’s leadership believes that the city’s defenses will be sufficient to protect its most valuable inhabitants, just as a cooking pot protects the desirable meat inside it. The unwanted scraps (the exiles), however, are thrown into the fire.

The city’s defenses (the cauldron) will not protect the inhabitants of Jerusalem (the meat). As they were once brought out of Egypt and delivered from the hands of the Egyptians, now they will be driven out of the land and delivered into the hands of foreigners who are themselves the agents of the Lord’s judgment.

Ironically, this name means “Yahweh provides escape.” Just as in ch. 9, Ezekiel sees the judgment that the Lord has pronounced immediately being enacted. When this man dies suddenly and unexpectedly during Ezekiel’s vision, Ezek­iel fears that all hope of escape has died with him, causing Ezekiel to pose the same question as in 9:8.

Instead of the usual term, this is literally “the men of your redemption,” that is, close relatives who act to preserve the family and property in case of an emergency such as bankruptcy (Ruth 2:20 note). In the case of Ezekiel and his fellow exiles, entire families have been transported, leaving no one in Judah to guard the inheritance. However, God Himself will be their protector.

Since the exiles are far from the temple in Jerusalem, God Himself will substitute as their sanctuary. The Lord has not simply departed _from_ the sanctuary in Jerusalem; He has departed _to_ the exiles in order to identify with them in their sufferings. Jesus later takes the place of the temple (Matt. 26:61; 27:40; John 2:19), and through the Spirit His followers become His temple (1 Cor. 3:16, 17; 2 Cor. 6:16; 1 Pet. 2:5).

The exile in Babylon will not be permanent. After God’s judgment is complete, He will bring His remnant back in a new exodus to Israel. The Lord will also change them on the inside, giving them an undivided heart of loyalty to the Lord and a new, responsive spirit in place of their old hearts of stone. This inner transformation in their hearts will lead to new levels of obedience to the Lord’s statutes and rules. The goal of the covenant will be achieved: God dwelling in the midst of His holy people. This is the first clear indication of hope in the book of Ezekiel.

According to the book of Hebrews, the new heart and new spirit promised here to God’s old covenant people have been received by His new covenant people—all those who trust in Christ alone for salvation (Heb. 8:8–13). As the Spirit renews believers’ thinking, God enables them to put off old ways of disobedience and to put on new acts of faithfulness to Him (Eph. 4:22–24). If anyone is in Christ, he is new creation (2 Cor. 5:17).

At the close of his vision, Ezekiel sees the glory cloud depart from the city of Jerusalem and move east across the Kidron Valley to the Mount of Olives as it departs from the city. But God has not forsaken the city forever. Ezekiel later describes the glory of God returning to Jerusalem (ch. 43). In the meantime, the Spirit of God returns the prophet to Babylon so that he can communicate this vision to the people there.

Another sign-act (4:1–3 note). The prophet depicts the exile of his countrymen who have remained in Jerusalem by packing a few precious articles to carry, as if he were a refugee, and digging through the wall, as if seeking to escape from a besieged city without being noticed.

See 2:3–8; 3:9, 26, 27. The inhabi­tants of the land of Judah are not the only rebels; the exiles among whom Ezekiel lives have the same heart issue.

**eyes ... ears.** Cf. Deut. 29:4; Prov. 20:12; Is. 6:9, 10; 32:3; Jer. 5:21; Matt. 13:15, 16; Mark 8:18; Acts 28:26, 27; Rom. 11:8. The entire section frequently alludes to seeing (vv. 4–7, 12, 13).

Digging through the wall of a house under cover of darkness represents a furtive escape (v. 5). Ezekiel vividly portrays Zedekiah’s abortive effort to escape from Nebuchadnezzar (vv. 10, 11; 2 Kin. 25:3–7). Compare with the exodus (see Ex. 12:11).

Covering the face is a gesture of shame or grief (24:17, 22; cf. Lev. 13:45; 2 Sam. 19:4; Esth. 6:12; 7:8; Pss. 44:15; 69:7). In this context, it suggests that the exiles will never see Jerusalem again, and more particularly, that Zedekiah will lose his sight (vv. 12, 13; 2 Kin. 25:7).

God is described as a hunter or fowler (17:20; 32:3; cf. Job 19:6; Is. 8:14; 24:18; 51:20; Jer. 50:24; Lam. 1:13; Hos. 7:12). Zedekiah’s tragic end is not simply the result of Babylonian expansionism but the Lord’s act of judgment. Only a handful of those who have remained in Judah would escape. These will declare their abominations to their captors by acknowledging the justice of God’s judgment.

Another sign-act (Introduction: Genre and Literary Features). The prophet is to tremble in fear as he eats his food and drinks his water, representing the terror that the inhabitants of Jerusalem will feel as they see their doom approaching. The exiles in Babylon are actually the fortunate ones, not those who have been left behind in Jerusalem.

These passages are united by a concern with false prophecy. The OT uses a number of criteria for distinguishing true from false prophecy. These criteria focus on what the message is, how it is received, and who receives it. (1) The preeminent criterion for true or false prophecy is the fulfillment of the prophet’s words (Deut. 18:21, 22). His message must not contradict earlier revelation (Deut. 13:1–5). The message of a true prophet often runs against popular sentiment, and true prophets are regularly persecuted because of their unpopular pronouncements (Jer. 20:7–10; 38:1–13; cf. Matt. 23:34, 35). (2) Certain means of discerning God’s will are forbidden (Deut. 18:9–14), including divination, spiritism, and sorcery. However, prophets can receive revelation through dreams and visions (Num. 12:6–8). (3) The true prophet is admitted to God’s confidence (Jer. 23:18). The experience of admission to God’s councilas if to a divine assembly is often reported in a call narrative (1:4–3:15 note). Finally, the prophet’s character must be consistent with the glory of the God he serves. It is not always easy to distinguish true from false prophecy at the time it is given, as false prophets can make all sorts of claims (1 Kin. 22) and prophecies are not always fulfilled immediately.

The first popular slogan about prophecy is that time is passing and the visions are not coming to pass. Therefore, the people conclude that the prophets can safely be ignored. However, the Lord declares that all of the prophecies will be fulfilled. He will eliminate false visions and then soon bring about the true visions that He has given to His prophets.

The people scoff that the prophecy will not be fulfilled in their lifetimes. The people have seen prophecies of judgment go unfulfilled for so long that they assume such prophecies are always about the distant future. That has led the people to the false assumption that the words of a prophet are always for the distant future. In the NT, a similar attitude of disbelief does not change the certainty of the return of Christ (2 Pet. 3:3, 4, 10; Rev. 10:6, 7).

False prophets invent their own prophecies, while true prophets can speak only the words the Lord gives them. In this case, though, the false prophets will receive a true word from the Lord—ironically, a word declaring their own destruction (vv. 4–23).
A word used by the prophets in declarations of divine judgment.

The prophet describes the false prophets as being like jackals among ruins. These animals are not simply useless to Judean society but harmful as they scavenge food for themselves (cf. the “fox” in Neh. 4:3). These prophets claim to have a word from God, but their visions are false and their words are lies.

verse_quote: not gone up into the breaches.
note: The true prophet is willing to expose himself to risk on behalf of God’s people. When an attacking army breaches a wall around a city in Ezekiel’s day, the most dangerous assignment is repairing the gap. At such points, the false prophets are nowhere to be found; they are more interested in their own safety than the good of the people. The Hb. term for a gap is also used to describe Moses, who “stood in the breach” (Ps. 106:23) on behalf of Israel. Ultimately only Jesus Christ, the final prophet, can stand in the breach between God and humanity (1 Tim. 2:5).

Probably the census list and civil register of Israel, the earthly counterpart of the heavenly records. See note on 9:2. The false prophets will not be listed among those who return to Judah after the exile (see Ezra 2). They have proclaimed “peace,” when there is no peace to be found (cf. Jer. 6:14; 8:11).

Their false visions and lying divinations make these prophets like people who conceal the shoddy workmanship of a wall under a coat of whitewash (v. 10 text note). The wall might look substantial, but it cannot withstand the flood of God’s judgment, the day of the Lord when God Himself will bring judgment on the city. When it falls, it will destroy the false prophets along with it.

The Bible mentions several true prophetesses, including Miriam, Deborah, Huldah, and Anna (Ex. 15:20; Judg. 4:4; 2 Kin. 22:14; 2 Chr. 34:22; Luke 2:36), as well as some false ones (Neh. 6:14; Rev. 2:20). The problem for Ezekiel in this passage is not that women are prophesying but that they are practicing magic and sorcery, activities specifically forbidden for Israel (12:21–14:11 note). They make their living by selling amulets and charms in exchange for small amounts of food, promising the power of life and deathto those who pay them. Such power belongs to true prophets as they proclaim God’s words (3:17–21; 33:1–9). The marketing tactics of these prophetesses discourages the righteous and encourages the wicked by declaring that judgment or acceptance by God depends on paying their fees, not on righteousness. The Lord will act to set His people free from their snare.
The leaders of the exiled community (see 8:1; 20:1). They visit the prophet, probably seeking a word of encouragement, but they instead hear a word of judgment.

One of the prophet’s favorite phrases (vv. 4, 7; 7:19; 44:12). The elders have set up idols in their hearts and are tainted with the very same sins that affect those left behind in Jerusalem (8:10–12). Though outwardly they are serving the Lord, their hearts are elsewhere; such divided devotion deserves no response from the Lord (Ps. 24:3, 4). In exile, the Babylonian gods form a significant temptation because of their apparent power to give victories to the Babylonian king, who successfully conquers many nations. The exiles don’t necessarily want to abandon the Lord; they simply want to access the power of these deities.

verse_quote: I ... have deceived ... I will stretch out my hand.
note: Numerous biblical passages integrate the sovereignty of God and the moral responsibility of human beings without allowing the predetermined will of God to be used as an excuse for moral evil (Esth. 4:13, 14; Joel 2:32; Matt. 26:24, 25; Acts 2:23). In this section, idolaters without any intention of giving up their idolatry come to seek a prophetic word. By God’s arrangement, they find a prophet as false as they are, and both will come under God’s judgment. The prophet who serves them, though ordained by God, bears the responsibility for his wrongdoing (cf. 1 Kin. 22:19–25). Yet the goal of the Lord’s acts of judgment is not to destroy the exiles but to deliver them from their heart idolatries. God’s sovereign plan to have a people to call His own cannot be thwarted.

The prophet is apparently addressing the view held by some that the presence of a certain minimal number of righteous people in Jerusalem will serve to protect the city (cf. Gen. 18:22–32). Although Ezekiel speaks of a hypothetical country, it is clear that Israel is in view since it is the only nation that has a covenant relationship with the Lord. If the nation breaks the conditions of its covenant, then it cannot complain if it experiences the curses specified in the covenant. These covenant curses are itemized in the form of four test cases, using four curses from the list in Lev. 26: famine (vv. 13, 14; Lev. 26:26), wild animals (vv. 15, 16; Lev. 26:22), war (vv. 17, 18; Lev. 26:25), and disease (vv. 14:19, 20; Lev. 26:25).

Though Noah was a righteous man and blameless among those of his generation (Gen. 6:9), the world was not spared because of his presence. Job, too, was blameless and upright (Job 1:1), but this did not spare his family. The identity of the Daniel mentioned is much debated. The Hb. spelling used here (Daniel) is different from that used for the name of the prophet Daniel, who was Ezekiel’s contemporary (Daniyyel), so some have assumed that Ezekiel is referring to a similarly named pagan heroic figure mentioned in an ancient Ugaritic text. However, such minor variations in the spelling of biblical names are extremely common, and it is unlikely that a true prophet like Ezekiel would pick a well-known pagan as a model of covenantal righteousness and wisdom. Each of the three biblical characters is famous for faithfulness in the midst of difficult circumstances. Yet even if the land contains not one but three such men, their righteousness cannot save the city of Jerusalem (cf. v. 20). How much more hopeless is Jerusalem’s condition, then, since she not only lacks such a righteous man but is filled with unrighteousness, and so will be affected not by one but by all four curses at once. The city is doomed to almost complete destruction.
The first in a series of metaphors, each of which depicts Jerusalem’s imminent judgment.

The wood of the vine is not fit to make into any worthwhile object, not even a peg on which to hang something. It has no strength or beauty; it is good only for the fire. God reminds the exiles that His choice of Israel as His people is not because of any intrinsic worth in them, but solely a matter of His grace (Deut. 7:6–8).

If the wood of the vine is useless before it was burned, how much more useless will it be after it has been partially consumed by fire? The partial burning of Israel is probably a reference to the partial exile that took place in 597 B.C. with the deportation of Jehoiachin and a large portion of the city’s upper class, including Ezekiel. Even after this act of judgment, the city has not been redeemed but is actually worth even less. The prophet Zechariah likens the Babylonian exile to a fire when he describes the high priest as “a brand plucked from the fire” (Zech. 3:2). The vine metaphor is often used elsewhere as a symbol for Israel, expressing God’s personal care for His people as their gardener (Ps. 80:8, 9; Is. 5:1–7). Yet they have failed to return the good fruit that He expects from them (Is. 5:2; Jer. 2:21). Jesus is the true Vine that God Himself tends (John 15:1). He is thus the true Israel, and those who are in Him are the true, fruit-bearing community of God. On the other hand, those who are separated from Christ are worthless, fit only for the fire (John 15:5, 6)., 5
Like the land destined for judgment in ch. 14, Jerusalem has been unfaithful to the Lord and therefore faces judgment.

Ezekiel tells the story of an unwanted child, her marriage, and infidelity. Hosea also uses marriage as an analogy of the covenant relationship between God and Israel (Hos. 1–3; see also Eph. 5:22–33; Rev. 19:7; 21:2, 9). Ezekiel’s speech appears to have a judicial setting; he recounts God’s charge against the nation from its earliest days to his own time, revealing Jerusalem’s true nature as a wanton prostitute.

Jerusalem was originally a pagan city; the first inhabitants are variously described as Amorites, Canaanites, Jebusites, and Hittites (v. 45; cf. Gen. 10:15, 16; Josh. 10:5; Judg. 1:21; 19:10, 11; 2 Sam. 5:6). It was not conquered in the days of Joshua, and it has retained a significant Canaanite population even after David finally captured it.

Her parents did not perform the usual birth practices of cutting the umbilical cord, washing her, smearing her body with salt and oil, and swaddling her in tightly wrapped cloths. Instead, she was left exposed in a field to die, as happened regularly in antiquity to unwanted baby girls.
The Lord found her in this hopeless state and rescued her through His life-giving words.

The unwanted child grew up to be beautiful. The onset of puberty appeared with development of breasts (cf. 23:3) and the growth of hair; later the girl reached the age of sexual maturity (v. 8). In terms of the metaphor, the Lord blessed Jerusalem even prior to her becoming an Israelite city.

verse_quote: spread the corner of my garment over you.
note:
Covering a woman with one’s garment is symbolic of entering into marital relations (Ruth 3:9). To “uncover” this relation is to violate it (Deut. 22:30).

**I made my vow.** The covenant relationship of God with Israel was sealed with the oath, “you shall be my people, and I will be your God” (36:28; Lev. 26:12; Jer. 11:4; 30:22; cf. Hos. 1:9). For the divine oath, see Gen. 15:7–21; 26:3; Deut. 1:8. This relates to the Davidic covenant, which has meant the election of Jerusalem as well as that of David and his descendants (Ps. 132).

The foundling becomes a queen. She has received all the care she lacked when born and far more. Her life, status, wealth, and beauty all derive from the gracious gift of the One who has chosen her. He has provided beautiful jewelry for her and the finest of foods, which has led to her fame spreading throughout the world.

All that the foundling-become-queen received from her loving husband and king is now turned to wantonness and promiscuity (cf. Deut. 6:10–12). She has thought that her beauty and splendor were her own achievements, not gifts from the Lord. She has given her clothes and jewels to her idols, along with the food with which the Lord had blessed her (cf. Hos. 2). Her actions demonstrate the irrationality of sin; there can be no sound reason for such behavior.

For the practice of child sacrifice in Israel and among neighboring states, see v. 36; 20:31; cf. Lev. 18:21; 20:2–5; Deut. 12:31; 18:10; 2 Kin. 16:3; 17:17; 21:6; 23:10; Ps. 106:37, 38; Jer. 32:35; Mic. 6:7. In Jerusalem, these practices are associated with the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, south of the city.

Many of the prophets depict idolatry as adultery (e.g., Hos. 2), yet Ezekiel takes the illustration much further. Jerusalem acts like a prostitute, committing adultery on every street corner with an inexhaustible appetite for more. Instead of demanding payment for her services, like most prostitutes, Jerusalem herself has given gifts to her lovers (v. 33). Israel’s failure to obey God is not a matter of idolatry alone. Foreign alliances with Egypt, Assyria, and Babylon are also regarded as evidence of failure to trust God in the face of political difficulty. Such alliances were a breach of Israel’s exclusive allegiance to the Lord (cf. 23:7; 29:16; cf. Is. 7; 8; 30; 31; Jer. 2:36, 37; 22:20–22; Hos. 7:11–13). The writer of Chronicles emphasized this point particularly (2 Chr. 14:9–15; 16:1–9; 19:1, 2; 20; 25:6–8; 28).

Ezekiel’s language is deliberately graphic and offensive here, even more in the Hebrew than in most English translations. That offensiveness is precisely the point of the passage; the prophet will not be polite and restrained about the nation’s sin that is about to bring such devastating destruction upon their heads.

She has sought the loyalty and affection of her lovers, but instead they have become the instruments of her humiliation and punishment. Though God uses the nations to punish His people, those nations will bear the guilt of the sins they have committed (ch. 25; cf. Is. 10:5, 12; Zech. 1:14, 15); see note on 14:9.

**uncover your nakedness.** Public degradation by exposing the nakedness of prostitutes or adulteresses is also mentioned in Jer. 13:22, 26; Hos. 2:10; Nah. 3:5.

For the wrath of a jealous husband, see Prov. 6:34. The wealth and garments of the woman will be taken, and she will be left as naked as she was when the story began. She will be covered not with the blood of childbirth (v. 6) but the blood from her wounds. According to the Mosaic law, adultery is a capital offense that is punishable by stoning (Lev. 20:10; Deut. 22:21–24; cf. John 7:53–8:11).

See 23:47; cf. Jer. 32:29; 34:22; 37:8; 38:18. Her houses will be burned, along with the destruction of her pagan shrines (v. 39). The Babylonian army burns a large part of Jerusalem when it finally takes the city in 586 B.C. (Jer. 39:8).
Ezekiel more than once refers to popular proverbs (12:21–28; 18). The metaphor shifts at this point from husband and wife to parent and daughters.
The Hittites and Amorites were the previous inhabitants of the Promised Land who were expelled from the land for their sins (Gen. 15:16). Jerusalem bears their family likeness.
Home of corrupt worship since the days of Jeroboam, who built shrines for his golden calves at Bethel and Dan (1 Kin. 12:28–33).

Readers of the Bible often think of the sins of Sodom as mainly sexual (Gen. 19:5–9). While Sodom was guilty of sexual sins such as homosexuality and sexual violence, Ezekiel also indicts the city for its materialism and its neglect of the poor and needy. Jesus makes a similar comparison with Capernaum in Matt. 11:23, 24. The sins of Jerusalem exceed those of her sisters, the nearby cities Sod­om and Samaria. In comparison to Jerusalem, Sod­om and Samaria seem virtuous. Both Sodom and Samaria were destroyed for their sins, so Jerusalem must inevitably face the same fate.

The Lord’s decision to destroy Jerusalem for her sins is vindicated. Yet He will also restore Jerusalem, along with her sin-laden sisters, so that Jerusalem’s pride will be crushed and she will feel appropriate shame for her actions.

Though Jerusalem has broken her covenant comprehensively, the Lord promises a new covenant, a new relationship between God and the city in the future. God Himself will atone for her sins and restore her entirely by His grace, so that there will be no room left for her to boast any more.

This oracle has no date, but is probably delivered sometime between the dates given in 8:1 and 20:1, the sixth and seventh years of the exile of Jehoiachin (592–590 B.C.). Nebuchadnezzar lays siege to Jerusalem in 587 B.C. and removes Zedekiah from the throne in 586 B.C. (v. 20). For Zedekiah’s demise, see 2 Kin. 24; 25; 2 Chr. 36; Jer. 52).

**17:1–24** Ezekiel propounds a riddle, or more precisely a fable, a story that transports elements from the real world into the world of animals and plants. The fantasy context distances the story from the reality, which enables the force of its message to penetrate the defenses of a resistant audience.

The imperial might of Babylon, represented by Nebuchadnezzar.

**cedar.** Represents the kingdom of Judah and the dynasty of David that has endured over three hundred years by this time.
The removal of the topmost twig refers to the exile and captivity of Jehoiachin in Babylon. The exiles continue to regard Jehoiachin as the legitimate king of Judah.

Nebuchadnezzar replaces the cedar with the far more humble and lowly vine, a reference to his installation of Zedekiah on the throne in Jerusalem after deporting Jehoiachin (2 Kin. 24:15–17). Nebuchadnezzar has done much for Zedekiah, just as the vine has fertile soil and abundant water, and prospered., 6
The turning of the vine toward another great eagle represents Zed­ekiah’s shift in allegiance from Nebuchadnezzar to Egypt (vv. 15–17), resulting in the vine itself being uprooted and destroyed.

In Judah, the east wind blows off the desert and is therefore hot and dry, withering vegetation in its path (see 19:12). The Lord’s judgment in the shape of Babylon will uproot and wither the Davidic line. Since it is a riddle, the surface meaning does not exhaust its significance. The vine planted in perfect conditions is also a classic picture of Israel, while the eagle that cares so tenderly for the vine actually seems to describe the Lord’s care more than Nebuchadnezzar’s. This underlines the analogy between Zedekiah’s rebellion against his covenant overlord, Nebuchadnezzar, and Israel’s rebellion against the Lord. If Zedekiah’s rebellion against Babylon is suicidal, as the fable clearly demonstrates, what does that say about Israel’s treason against her master?

Although the OT histories do not record Zedekiah’s appeal to Egypt for help, Jeremiah does mention it (Jer. 37:5–11; 44:30). One of the Lachish letters, written on broken pottery in the last days of the kingdom of Judah, reports that a commander of the army went down to Egypt, perhaps to ask for help. See 16:26; 29:6, 7; 30:20–26.

The last part of the chapter gives the fable an unexpected twist. The Bible often uses a tree as a symbol of royalty (Dan. 4:9–12, 19–22), particularly as a figure of the Messiah. The messianic Branch will be a fresh start from the house of David (Is. 4:2; 11:1; 53:2; 60:21; Jer. 23:5; 33:15; Zech. 6:12). Ezekiel announces that though the present line of David has reached a dead end in Zedekiah, someday God will take a descendant of Jehoiachin (cf. vv. 3, 4 and 12, 13) and restore him to kingship in Judah.

Rather than being dependent upon other kingdoms (birds like the eagles), this splendid cedar will become a haven for birds of all kinds (cf. Dan. 4:12, 21). This tree will be fruitful in a way that the first cedar has never been (2 Kin. 19:30; cf. Is. 11:1; 37:31; Jer. 17:8; cf. John 15:4, 5, 8, 16).

The exile is not the result of the sins of a single generation. Rather, the continued disobedience of Israel through many generations “since the day their fathers came out of Egypt, even to this day” (2 Kin. 21:15) finally brings judgment on Judah. God judges the cumulative guilt of the nation in the events that lead up to the destruction of Jerusalem. The response of the exiles is to question the justice of God. The popular proverb (v. 2; cf. Jer. 31:29) in effect says, “It’s not our fault—we are being punished for what we did not do. Our fathers sinned, and we are the ones who are paying the price” (cf. Lam. 5:7). Ezekiel replies by emphasizing that God responds according to the acts of each individual and generation. The exiles cannot evade their guilt; they are suffering for their own sins as well (Deut. 24:16). The prophet builds his argument as a case study involving three consecutive generations. He describes a righteous man with an unrighteous son but a repentant and righteous grandson. Each one is measured against exactly the same list of moral behaviors, and each receives precisely what he deserves.

Refers to participating in sacrificial meals in the presence of pagan gods at the high places (6:13; 20:28; 22:9; cf. Ex. 32:5, 6).

**impurity.** The law prohibits sexual intercourse during a woman’s period, when she is ceremonially unclean (22:10; cf. Lev. 15:16–33; 18:19). Emissions of bodily life fluids make a person ritually impure, and contact with those emissions renders others impure as well.

See vv. 12, 16; cf. Ex. 22:26; Deut. 24:10–13, 17; Prov. 20:16; Amos 2:8. Lending money with interest is outlawed in the OT because of the opportunity it provides for extortion. The poor might give up an object as security that the loan will be repaid, but if that object is an outer garment, it must be returned before nightfall to protect him against the cold. An ostracon (a piece of broken pottery with writing on it) of the late seventh century B.C. records the complaint of a field worker to a village official that his employer had taken his garment and kept it., 8

Having a righteous father does not mean the unrighteous son will escape punishment for his sin. The son deliberately transgresses the law in all of the ways that his father kept it. God will not allow Himself to be merely an escape hatch in times of trouble; He cannot be looked to as Savior without also being received as Lord. Outward behavior often reveals a person’s heart more clearly and accurately than his or her words do (Luke 6:43–45).
Conversely, having an unrighteous father will not bring judgment on a righteous son (v. 10 note; Deut. 24:16; 2 Kin. 14:6).

If God judges each generation for their own sins, Ezekiel’s contemporaries are part of a generation that is under God’s judgment. Is there any hope for their future? Ezekiel adds two more case studies: wicked people who turn away from their sin and righteous people who abandon their faithfulness. Real change is possible if there is repentance. On the other hand, those who are in a right relationship with God need to persevere in faithfulness, not growing weary of doing what is right (Gal. 6:9). This is precisely why Ezekiel has been appointed as a watchman for Israel (ch. 3).

This is a summary statement. The fundamental problem for Israel, and for all people, is not God’s injustice but a lack of righteousness. The house of Israel thoroughly deserves God’s judgment; sin can never be taken lightly in one’s relationship with God. Yet within the solemn warnings about the gravity of sin and the threat it represents, there remains the assurance that God does not desire or delight in the death of the wicked (2 Pet. 3:9). God is both just and merciful, and all those who repent will find the way to life (2 Chr. 6:37–39; Is. 30:15; 59:20; Jer. 18:8; Matt. 4:17; Mark 1:4, 15; Luke 13:3, 5; 15:7, 10; 24:47; Acts 3:19; 17:30; 2 Cor. 7:10).

verse_quote: make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit.
note: Elsewhere God also commands what He alone can give (cf. Deut. 10:16 with 30:6). As Ezek­iel himself recognizes, the new heart and spirit are gifts of God (36:26) and not the product of human effort (cf. Eph. 2:8, 9). Ezekiel exhorts his audience to seek these not through their own merit but by repentance (v. 32).

Ezekiel presents another allegory using the kind of Hebrew poetry ordinarily used for funeral dirges and laments. This poetry has a particular meter that Ezekiel’s audience will recognize. The same rhythm is used in texts such as 26:17, 18; 28:12–19; 32:2–8. It is called the _qinah_, or dirge rhythm (Introduction to Lamentations: Genre and Literary Features). In this case, those being lamented are not yet dead. The lament affirms the certainty of their fate.

The lioness represents the nation of Israel or the city of Jerusalem, which has produced these cubs, or kings. (Cf. Ps. 87:5; Is. 50:1; 54:1; Gal. 4:26, 27 for the image of Jerusalem as mother.) The lion is frequently an image of Davidic kingship (Gen. 49:9; Mic. 5:8). The NT looks for “the Lion of the tribe of Judah” to reestablish the kingdom of God (Rev. 5:5).
Jehoahaz reigns for only three months before he is taken to Egypt as a captive of Pharaoh Neco in 609 B.C. His brief reign is characterized in purely negative terms (2 Kin. 23:31–34; 2 Chr. 36:2–4).

Ezekiel omits any description of the reign of Jehoiakim and proceeds to his son Jehoiachin (or possibly Zedekiah; both are exiled by Nebuchadnezzar). Second Kings does not mention any exile for Jehoiakim (2 Kin. 23:36–24:7; cf. 2 Chr. 36:5–8); he apparently died in Jerusalem.

Jehoiakim has rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar, and the wrath of the Babylonian king is directed against his son Jehoiachin. Ezekiel describes his deportation to Babylon in 597 B.C. (2 Kin. 24:8–16; 2 Chr. 36:9, 10). Jehoiachin is imprisoned until the reign of Evil-merodach (562–560 B.C.; 2 Kin. 25:27–30).
Like the lion, the vine in a vineyard is a familiar image for the royal tribe of Judah (see Is. 5:1–7). God planted it in perfect conditions by the water; thus, it grew strong.

As in 17:9, 10, the east wind is an instrument of Yahweh’s will (Ex. 10:13; 14:21; Ps. 78:26; Hos. 13:15; Jon. 4:8). The east wind brings the desert heat and will wither the vine. Judah’s pride leads to her uprooting, like the vine in ch. 17.

The end of the kingdom of Judah is described as a time when the vine is uprooted and no branch is left to make a ruler’s scepter. For the use of a branch as a symbol of the messianic king, see note on 17:22. The fire that has come from one of its branches (Zedekiah) consumes the fruit (the land and the people) and the other branches (the rest of the royal household). Even though at this time Zedekiah is not yet dead, his downfall is already so certain that it is time to sing his lament.

Once again the elders of the exiles gather to seek instruction from the prophet, about a year later than the date last mentioned (8:1; cf. 14:1). The date is the tenth of Ab (August 591 B.C.), five years to the day before Jerusalem is put to the torch (Jer. 52:12). Normally, inquiring of the Lord is a good thing, yet He has already condemned these people for their heart idolatry, and He refuses to receive their request. As a result, their question is not even recorded—only the Lord’s indictment of them.

The indictment beginsby recounting Israel’s constant history of unfaithfulness to the Lord. Like ch. 18, it is a story of three generations who had to choose between obeying the Lord’s life-giving laws or following the path of disobedience. These generations are successively the generation that experienced the exodus out of Egypt (vv. 5–9), the generation that spent a lifetime in the wilderness (vv. 10–17), and the generation after that (vv. 18–23). Each generation received the Lord’s statutes, especially the Sabbath commandment, whose rest was a sign of their deliverance out of Egypt. But each generation in turn rebelled against the Lord and violated His Sabbaths, trampling on the sign the Lord gave them. Each therefore experienced the curses of the covenant rather than its blessings, culminating in the Lord giving the third generation “statutes that were not good” (v. 25), so that they offered their firstborn sons to the god Molech (v. 26). This was the exact opposite of the goal of the exodus, which freed Israel, the Lord’s firstborn son (Ex. 4:22), from Egypt so that the people could offer pure worship in the Promised Land. The Lord sometimes hands over those who neglect His gracious revelation to their own depravity, with terrible consequences (see Rom. 1:18–25).
This phrase is repeated several times in the chapter (vv. 5, 6, 15, 23, 28, 42). God had pledged Himself to Israel and would perform His promises. See Ex. 3:6–10; 6:2–8.

The Pentateuch does not record details about the religious life of the Israelites during their slavery in Egypt, but it is safe to infer that they assimilated the religion of the culture there just as they did later in Canaan. The incident with the golden calf (Ex. 32) should be understood against the background of idolatry in Egypt. See 23:3; Josh. 24:14.

The law was God’s gracious gift to Israel; it was a way of life (Deut. 4:40; 32:46, 47; Josh. 1:7, 8). This is an allusion to Lev. 18:5, which in the OT and the NT stands as a single summary statement for the essence of the requirements of the law (cf. Rom. 10:5 and Gal. 3:12).

The Sabbath (vv. 13, 16, 21, 24) is singled out as a law unique to Israel, one that most clearly distinguished it from the nations. The Sabbath is often cited as an important example that stands for the whole law (22:8, 26; 23:38; 44:24; cf. Neh. 13:18; Is. 56:2, 4, 6; Jer. 17:19–27).

The first generation in the wilderness rebelled against God (Ex. 17:2; Num. 14:1–19; 16; 17; 20:10, 24; 25; 26:9; 27:14; Deut. 1:26, 43; 9:7; 31:27).

**my Sabbaths.** See Num. 15:32–36.

The threat of exile existed even before the people entered the land (Lev. 26:32–35; Deut. 28:64–67; Ps. 106:26, 27). Moses predicted that they would rebel against the Lord once in the land (Deut. 31:27, 29).
Possibly a statement summarizing the complaints of the people (cf. Num. 11:1).

The law is God’s gracious gift (v. 11 note), but when it is perverted it brings death. The practice of child sacrifice in ancient Israel was a perversion of their laws regarding the firstborn (Ex. 13:1, 2, 11–16; 22:29; 34:19, 20; Num. 18:15, 16). Every firstborn belonged to the Lord, and they were to be redeemed rather than sacrificed. In Jesus Christ, the Lord would substitute His own firstborn as the Lamb of God who redeems His people from the wrath of God (Col. 1:15–20; 1 Thess. 1:10; cf. Gen. 22).

Israel’s history of rebellion is reflected in the behavior of the present generation. Up to the prophet’s own day, the same patterns of idolatry and child sacrifice have continued. Such people cannot rightly expect to inquire of the Lord and hear from Him.
Second Kings measures almost every ruler of Judah in terms of what he did about the high places around Jerusalem, as they were the most obvious and blatant examples of public idolatry.

The desire to be like the surrounding nations (v. 32) reflects 1 Sam. 8:20; the people have rejected God (1 Sam. 8:7, 8), and so are facing judgment, just like the earlier generations in Ezekiel’s retelling of Israel’s history. But just as God did not abandon earlier generations of His chosen people, so now He promises a new exodus and a return to the wilderness experience (vv. 33–35). Just as only the faithful and obedient from the wilderness generation crossed into the land (Num. 14:30, 38), so will God again purge the nation to bring a faithful people into the land (vv. 36–38). The honor of God’s name demands that He fulfill His promises, even in the face of a history of unrelenting human sin. Israel cannot simply choose to be like the nations, for God has chosen the nation for Himself.
Refers to the desolation of exile, which Israel is experiencing. Israel is once again going to be judged in a “wilderness,” just as the wilderness generation was.
Alludes to the practice of counting off animals for the tithe (Lev. 27:32, 33). It suggests that only a tenth will be left (cf. Is. 6:13).
The goal of the periodic catastrophes that befall Israel is commonly to produce a purified, purged, and faithful remnant (6:8 note).

verse_quote: Go serve every one of you his idols.
note: Whether Israel chooses to rebel or to be faithful, God’s purpose to have a holy people for Himself cannot be thwarted. In the end, His people will worship Him in spirit and in truth (John 4:23, 24). The free choices humans make cannot thwart God’s sovereign purposes, which always prevail.

The faithful remnant will worship at God’s holy mountain, Zion. This foreshadows the vision of chs. 40–48, where the prophet sees the purified worship of God restored. The result of the new exodus will be something the first exodus was unable to achieve: pure worship, offered by a purified people who have been redeemed by the Lord’s sovereign grace. He deals with His people in mercy and not as our sins deserve (20:44; cf. Ezra 9:13; Job 33:27; Ps. 103:10; Lam. 3:22, 23, 31–33). With the coming of Christ, this worship is not offered on Mount Gerizim or even on Mount Zion, but wherever people gather in Jesus’ name (John 4:21).

This short prophecy against the south is the first of four sections, the last three of which are linked together by the catchword “sword,” which is an image of God’s judgment (see 21:1–7, 8–27, 28–32). The OT frequently describes God as a warrior. His sword is ordinarily wielded against Israel’s enemies (Deut. 32:41; Is. 31:8; 34:5–8; 66:16; Jer. 25:31; 50:35–37; Zeph. 2:12). But now the sword is given to the Babylonians to be wielded against Judah and Jerusalem.

Like all parables, this prophecy reveals and conceals. Some aspects of the parable are plain enough to anyone with eyes to see: it concerns an all-encompassing judgment that will consume every tree—not just the dry trees, which catch fire easily, but also the green trees, which are normally harder to set alight. It will cover the whole land, from south to north, and continue on indefinitely without being put out. Other aspects are not immediately clear: what is the “southland” that is being judged? The subsequent interpretation provides the missing information for the parable.

The image shifts from fire to the sword as the agent of judgment, but the message remains the same. The three terms for “south” in the parable are matched by three objects of judgment: Jerusalem, Israel, and her sanctuaries. It becomes clear that Israel is the “southland” from the perspective of her enemies, who traditionally come from the north (1:4 note). This time, however, the enemy is the Lord Himself, coming against her in judgment. This judgment will encompass righteous and wicked alike—the green and dry trees, respectively, of the parable.
The prophet is symbolically to groan in pain because of the coming judgment, which is described in terms identical to those in ch. 7.

verse_quote: A sword is sharpened and also polished.
note: These actions prepare the weapon for use, after which it is passed over to the executioner (v. 11).

These verses and v. 27 are united in part by their allusions to Judah’s scepter (Gen. 49:10). A wooden rod is nothing against an iron sword, and Judah is no contest for Nebuchadnezzar. However, the translation of v. 10 is uncertain. What is clear is the inevitability of the coming judgment., 13

The sword of the Lord is the sword of the king of Babylon. Ezekiel probably draws a map that looks something like an inverted “Y” scratched in the dirt or on a brick (4:1–3 note). Nebuchadnezzar will be coming from the north, approaching a fork in the road. The eastern fork will take the Babylonian armies down the King’s Highway, a major highway passing through modern-day Jordan. The western fork will take the Babylonians down the Via Maris, an important international highway on the coastal plain west of Jerusalem. One choice of route will take him to Rabbah, the capital of the Ammonites, while the other will bring him near Jerusalem.

The Babylonian king uses several ways to obtain guidance from the gods: (1) consulting the “teraphim,” religious objects used in worship; (2) divination by examining the contours and markings on the livers of sacrificed birds or sheep (hepatoscopy); (3) using arrows as a means of casting lots. The Lord will use the false divination, to which His people are so addicted (see 13:7), to persuade the pagan king to do His holy will.
The Judeans swore oaths of loyalty to Nebuchadnezzar, but they have been unfaithful to their commitments. In response, Nebuchadnezzar lays siege to Jerusalem by January 587 B.C.

verse_quote: O profane wicked one ... take off the crown.
note: The profane and wicked prince is Zed­ekiah, the last king of Judah (17:1–10 note). By not mentioning his name, the prophet makes it clear that it is the office that is under judgment, not just Zedekiah himself. The turban and the crown, the emblems of royalty, will be stripped away, bringing low the one who was once exalted., 26

verse_quote: the one to whom judgment belongs.
note: This oracle reshapes the traditional messianic promise of Gen. 49:10 into a word of judgment: the one who comes is Nebuchadnezzar, appointed by God for the judgment of His people (see 23:24).

From vv. 18–23 it might seem that the Babylonians will attack Jerusalem but spare Ammon. This third and last sword song explains that Ammon will likewise taste God’s wrath in the fury of the Babylonians (Jer. 49:1–6). Though judgment begins with the house of God, it does not end there. Ammon was allied with Jerusalem and Egypt against the Babylonians in 588 B.C. However, when Jerusalem comes under attack, Ammon takes advantage of the weakness of her former ally (Jer. 40:11, 14; 41:10, 15; cf. 2 Kin. 24:2).

Once Bab­ylon’s work as God’s agent of judgment is complete, the empire will experience the Lord’s judgment at home. Their sins, too, will be judged, even though the Lord has used them as the tool of His judgment.

This first of three oracles in ch. 22 revolves around repeated references to blood (vv. 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 13; cf. v. 27). The prophet acts as prosecuting counsel as the city of Jerusalem is indicted for both moral and ritual crimes. The charges are primarily drawn from Lev. 18–20, 25.

They abuse their own parents, breaking the fifth commandment (Deut. 5:16; Mic. 7:6; Rom. 1:30; Eph. 6:1; Col. 3:20; 2 Tim. 3:2) as well as the command against murder and the command to remember the Sabbath.

**the sojourner ... the fatherless and the widow.** See note on Ps. 9:18. See also Deut. 10:18; 14:29; 24:17; 26:12, 13; 27:19; Pss. 68:5; 72:4; 146:9; Is. 1:17; 10:1, 2; Jer. 7:6, 7; 22:3; Zech. 7:10; Mal. 3:5).
To uncover a father’s nakedness means to have sexual relations with his wife. For the range of forbidden sexual relations, see Lev. 18:6–23; 20:10–21.
Judah’s various sins are symptoms of a deeper problem: they have forgotten the Lord. Deut. 8:19 declares, “If you forget the Lord your God ... you shall surely perish.”
An angry gesture that precedes the Lord’s judgment of scattering His people. Instead of being the Lord’s holy people, they will be profaned.

Judah will be gathered into Jerusalem for judgment, just as metal is gathered in a smelter’s furnace. Normally, gathering is a good thing in the OT, the precursor to blessing. So, too, the image of a refiner’s fire is often a positive picture of a divine judgment on Israel designed to purge her of sin and to produce a pure people (6:8 note). Israel’s experience in Egypt is likened to time in a furnace (Deut. 4:20; 1 Kin. 8:51; Jer. 11:4), and the exile will be a refiner’s furnace for Israel (cf. Pss. 66:10; 119:119; Prov. 17:3; 25:4; Is. 1:25; 48:10; Jer. 9:7; Zech. 13:9; Mal. 3:2, 3; 1 Cor. 3:12–15; 1 Pet. 1:7). Yet if only dross goes into the fire, nothing positive will emerge.

All of the previous judgments have failed to purify the land; she is still polluted. The list of sins here is drawn from Zeph. 3:3, 4, where the focus is on the sins of the leaders of Judah: the princes, priests, leaders, and prophets. All of these groups have failed, resulting in the people going astray.

See note on 13:5. The Lord has sought someone to rebuild the wall and stand in the breach, as Moses did after the people sinned with the golden calf.
