In this case, however, the Lord finds no one to deflect His wrath, and so His fury will be poured out on them in full measure. Instead of confronting the people’s sin, the prophets speak false visions, whitewashing a flimsy wall instead of fortifying a real line of defense (see 13:10–12).

**22:31 I have returned their way upon their heads.** See 11:21.

As in ch. 16, Ezekiel describes the history of Israel and Judah in the form of an extended and graphic metaphor. The tale of two immoral sisters is the tale of two cities: “Oholah” is Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom, and “Oholibah” is Jerusalem, the capital of the southern kingdom. Even their names sound alike, and their stories and fates are similarly intertwined.

The indictment of the two kingdoms begins with their prostitution in their earliest days in Egypt (16:26; 20:5–9). Even before their marriage to the Lord, these two sisters displayed their true nature. Yet the Lord nonetheless chose them to be His. Marriage is a key biblical metaphor for the Lord’s covenant relationship with His people, which makes their pursuit of idols a form of adultery (cf. Hos. 1–3).

Israel’s oath of exclusive allegiance to the Lord at the time of the exodus (cf. Ex. 24) would be broken by foreign alliances as well as by idolatry (vv. 5–10; 16:26 note; cf. Hos. 8:9). Alliances with Assyria were part of Israel’s political strategy from the mid-eighth century B.C. Prostitution did not secure the admiration or affection of the Assyrian lovers—quite the contrary (vv. 9, 10). Ultimately Assyria destroyed the northern kingdom in 722 B.C. and scattered her people throughout the Assyrian empire (2 Kin. 17:5, 6).
The northern kingdom’s fate is already old history at this point. The prophet’s focus is the forthcoming (and matching) fate of Judah, the younger sister.

Judah is not merely like Israel—she is worse. She sinned in the same way with the Assyrians before transferring her loyalty to the Babylonians (2 Kin. 20:12–18; 23:29; Is. 39:1). She has also made overtures to Egypt (23:19–21).She has not been seduced merely by passing strangers; she herself has sent for the Babylonians to satisfy her lust. In fact, Judah’s pursuit of pleasure has gone beyond the human level to positively bestial depths (v. 20). What the Judean kings have regarded as wise political strategy, the Lord condemns as wanton adultery. When they remember Egypt, they recall the forbidden pleasures of that time instead of thinking about the Lord’s deliverance in the exodus. The result of such depravity is inevitable judgment. The nations she has courted will come and abuse her.
Perhaps Aramean tribes east of the Tigris River. These obscure nations are probably chosen because their names not only rhyme in Hebrew, but they sound like “Punishment, War Cry, and Shriek.”

See 16:35–41. What the adulterous wife (Judah) has done in private is now done to her publicly. In this case, since her adultery is worse than her sister’s, so too will her punishment be. She will not only be stripped but physically disfigured with her nose and ears cut off., 26

The cup is a common metaphor in the Bible. In many cases it is symbolic of God’s blessings (Pss. 16:5; 23:5; 116:13; 1 Cor. 10:16). It can also represent God’s anger (Ps. 75:7, 8; Is. 51:17–20; Jer. 25:15–29; 49:12; 51:7; Lam. 4:21; Hab. 2:16; Zech. 12:2; Rev. 14:9–11). In this case, it is a bitter cup of judgment. Jesus mentions this cup of wrath in the garden of Gethsemane (Matt. 26:39, 42), and it appears in John’s account of Jesus’ death (John 18:11; 19:28–30).
As if to rid herself of the parts of her anatomy that earlier were the seat of her pleasure (v. 21).

Ezekiel once again takes on the role of prosecuting attorney, convicting Jerusalem for her sins (see 22:2). In addition to the political unfaithfulness mentioned earlier, she has committed other cultic sins as well. Far from being the beautiful holy city, Jerusalem has become an old and worn-out prostitute. Once again, the historical reality appears through the metaphor: the adulteresses will not only be stoned but will be killed with swords and their houses burned.

**24:1–14** Ezekiel provides another allegory, that of a cooking pot. Two oracles applying it are introduced by the same phrase: “Woe to the bloody city” (vv. 6, 9).

The date of the beginning of the siege of the city is ordinarily identified as January 15, 587 B.C. (cf. 2 Kin. 25:1; Jer. 52:4). The date formula here does not match the sequence in the rest of the book but rather corresponds exactly to that in 2 Kings. The event that Ezekiel has warned about finally arrives. Literally, the Hb. word translated “laid siege” indicates that Nebuchadnezzar “leaned on” Jerusalem. This same word is used for a worshiper pressing his hands on an animal brought to be sacrificed (Lev. 1:4; 3:2). Jerusalem thus becomes a lamb being sacrificed, though she is far from being without blemish., 2

Ezekiel has already used the image of a cooking pot in 11:2–12 (cf. Jer. 1:13, 14; Mic. 3:3). From the initial description, it appears that preparations are being made for a festive meal in which the best of meats are to be cooked. Yet what ought to be a tasty meal turns out to be a foul mess. The choice meat that goes in comes out uniformly bad.

The pot, too, is rusty and beyond cleansing. The prophet likens the corrosion to the bloodshed and guilt in the city. Though its occupants are removed piece by piece and dispersed to the far corners of the world, the guilt of the city remains like scum in the bottom of the pot. Compare the denunciation of the bloodshed in the city in 22:1–16; 36:18. Cf. 2 Kin. 21:16; 24:4; Is. 26:21; 59:7; Lam. 4:13; Hos. 4:2; Joel 3:21; Mic. 3:10.
Blood, shed and uncovered, cries out to be avenged; note the same concept in Gen. 4:10; Job 16:18. The Lord will pour out her blood uncovered on a bare rock as vengeance., 8

The cauldron is boiled dry in a vain effort to cleanse it, but the scum is so resistant that even heating the cauldron white-hot will not purify it. Jerusalem’s impurity is indelible, and so God will have to destroy the city.

The prophets’ personal lives are often intertwined with their messages. Hosea was commanded to marry a prostitute (Hos. 1–3), while Isaiah was commanded to walk naked and barefoot for three years (Is. 20:2–5). In Ezekiel’s case, when his wife dies he is forbidden to follow the customary mourning practices, which include lamenting and crying; removing headgear and covering the head with dust and ashes (Josh. 7:6; 1 Sam. 4:12; Job 2:12); removing sandals (2 Sam. 15:30; Is. 20:2); and covering the head or face (Esth. 6:12; Jer. 14:3, 4). Ezekiel is to behave outwardly as if nothing has happened even though his heart must be in deep turmoil.

Ezekiel’s strange behavior has the desired effect of rousing the curiosity of the people. His response is that this is a sign: God is about to take away the temple, which is the delight of their eyes, desecrating it and destroying the sons and the daughters that many of them have left behind in Jerusalem. Yet on that day, the scale of the loss will be so overwhelming, affecting almost every individual, that there will be no possibility of performing normal mourning rites.

See 3:26 and note. Ezekiel’s message will be vindicated when word reaches the exiles that Jerusalem has been destroyed, and on that very day he will be released from the silence God has imposed on him. He will then once again be able to speak words of hope to the remnant of the exiles.

Between warnings of the destruction of Jerusalem (chs. 1–24) and prophecies of hope and restoration (chs. 33–48), Ezekiel includes a section of oracles against foreign nations. The nations denounced here by Ezekiel include six of Judah’s immediate neighbors in clockwise order, beginning with Ammon in the east (chs. 25–28) and concluding with a climactic seventh oracle against Egypt (chs. 29–32). The function of these oracles is to encourage God’s own people, to whom they are spoken, by assuring them of judgment on those who have assaulted them. If this negative side of the Abrahamic covenant is still in place (“those who dishonor you, I will curse”; Gen. 12:3), then the positive hope of blessing for Israel is still alive.

**25:1–7** Ezekiel has already spoken against Ammon (21:28–32). Israel and Judah’s relationship with the Ammonites is long and varied, primarily a record of conflict. Oracles against Ammon are also found in Jer. 49:1–6; Amos 1:13–15; Zeph. 2:8, 9. The Ammon­ites are charged with gloating over Judah’s downfall and celebrating the destruction of the temple.
See note on 6:7.

The punishment fits the crime: because they have rejoiced at the harm done to Jerusalem, the Ammonites themselves will become prey to a foreign power. Though many of the small states in the area escape destruction during the Babylonian invasion of 587–586 B.C., sources outside the Bible indicate that Nebuchadnezzar destroys Ammon and Moab in 582 B.C. The prophet makes the same point in 21:28–32., 7

Israel and Judah’s relationship with Moab is largely a history of conflict, and other prophets include oracles against this nation (Is. 15; 16; Jer. 48; Amos 2:1–3; Zeph. 2:8, 9). Moab has mocked Judah by saying, “Judah is like all the other nations,” which, ironically enough, is exactly how its inhabitants have been living (see 20:32). Yet given the Lord’s sovereign choice of His people, that statement can never ultimately be true. Unlike Judah, which will be restored, Moab will share Ammon’s fate of destruction.

Edom has gone further than Ammon and Moab and actually has made incursions into Judah at the time of Jerusalem’s fall (35:15; 36:5; Ps. 137:7–9; Lam. 4:21, 22). In the book of Obadiah, Edom is charged with cutting down fugitives and handing survivors back to the Babylonians (Obad. 11–14). The enmity between Israel and Edom is traced in the Bible to the hostile relationship between Jacob and Esau (Gen. 25:23, 30). Ezekiel includes a second oracle against Edom in ch. 35, and other prophets make pronouncements against this nation as well (Is. 34:5–11; Jer. 49:7–22; Amos 1:11, 12; Mal. 1:3–5).

The nations mentioned thus far are all east of the Jordan River and the Dead Sea. The Philistines occupy the coastal plain west of Judah, controlling a long segment of the vital international coastal highway. Conflicting territorial claims and competing strategic interests have made for a longstanding history of unfriendly relations with Israel and have led to unspecified crimes during the Babylonian assault. Ezekiel has already spoken of this enmity (16:27, 57). Other prophets also include oracles against the Philistines (Is. 14:29–31; Jer. 47; Joel 3:4–6; Amos 1:6–8; Zeph. 2:4–7; Zech. 9:5–7). The Philistines were Israel’s most prominent enemy during the rule of the judges and the united monarchy.

The Philistines appear to have entered Canaan in the latter half of the second millennium B.C. as part of the large migration of peoples known from Egyptian records as the “sea peoples.” One group of Philistines is identified as “Cherethites,” probably associating them with Crete. See note on 1 Sam. 30:14.

These chapters are devoted to oracles against Israel’s Phoenician neighbors, primarily Tyre (26:1–28:19) but also Sidon (28:20–26). The oracles against Tyre are divided into subsections, each introduced with the phrase “the word of the Lord came to me” and ending with the phrase “You have come to a dreadful end and shall be no more forever” (26:1–21; 27:1–36; 28:1–19). There was occasional military conflict between Israel and the Phoenicians, but the Bible mentions Tyre and Sidon more often as the source of pagan cults, especially the Baal worship that the Phoenicians supported (Judg. 10:6; 1 Kin. 11:1, 5, 33; 16:31; 2 Kin. 23:13). The Phoenicians provided Israel with trade and expert labor (2 Sam. 5:11; 1 Kin. 5:1, 6; 7:13, 14; 9:11; 2 Chr. 2:3, 13, 14; Ezra 3:7; Neh. 13:16; Acts 12:20). Other prophetic books also include oracles against Tyre and Sidon (Is. 23; Joel 3:4–6; Amos 1:9, 10; Zech. 9:2–4).

The kingdom of Judah at times controlled trade routes leading through the coastal plains to Egypt, as well as to Arabia and Africa via the port of Ezion Geber. Tyre stands to profit if Jerusalem loses control of these trade routes. Like her neighbors, therefore, Tyre has rejoiced over Jerusalem’s fall. However, she has not reckoned with Israel’s God. Instead of the way being opened up for trade, it will be opened up for nations coming against her for war. Like Jerusalem, she will be plundered by an invading army.

Shortly after the fall of Jerusalem, Neb­uchadnezzar lays siege to Tyre. The part of the city on the mainland falls quickly in 585 B.C., but the island fortress defies the armies of Babylon for thirteen years until 572 B.C. (29:17, 18). The detail with which Ezekiel describes the assault underlines the certainty of the outcome of the conflict. Tyre will end up as a bare rock, a desolate haunt for local fishermen, instead of the bustling metropolis that she has imagined becoming.

Tyre’s destruction will also affect all of her trading partners, who are located along the Mediterranean shoreline. They will mourn and sing songs of lament over her destruction, which will be as comprehensive as if the great city were to plunge to the depths of the ocean waves.

The Bible and other ancient Near Eastern texts commonly use “waters” as a metaphor for death (Ex. 15:5, 8, 10; Job 26:5; Pss. 32:6; 69:2, 14; Lam. 3:54), and the “pit” is a synonym for Sheol, the realm of the dead (31:14, 16; 32:18, 23, 24, 30; cf. Job 33:18–30; Pss. 30:3, 9; 55:23; 88:4–6; 103:4; 143:7; Prov. 1:12; Is. 14:15; 38:18). These two images are combined in 28:8; Ps. 69:15; Jon. 2:5, 6. The prophet describes these mythological waters of chaos engulfing the island and its inhabitants (28:2 note)., 21
The second oracle against Tyre is in the form of a funeral song comparing Tyre’s past glory to her impending destruction.

The island city of Tyre is likened to a luxurious ship made of the best materials and manned by an experienced crew drawn from all the surrounding areas. The geographical locations described in this section cover most of the known world in Ezekiel’s day. Senir is the Amorite name for Mount Hermon (Deut. 3:9). Elishah is part of Cyprus. Sidon, Arvad, and Gebal (Byblos) are coastal Mediterranean towns. Soldiers come from Persia to the east, Lud (Lydia) in Asia Minor to the north, and Put (Libya) to the south. Helech is Cilicia, the region around Tarsus, while Gamad is probably in northern Syria.

The great ship that represents Tyre has done business with a diverse range of customers. Tarshish is in the distant west, possibly part of Spain. Javan is Greece, while Tubal and Meshech are in Anatolia (modern-day Turkey), along with Beth-togarmah. Dedan is the coastal region north of Tyre. Minnith is a source of wheat in the Transjordan. Helbon is a town ten miles (16 km) north of Damascus, and Sahar may be located nearby. Uzal is likely in the foothills of Anatolia, while Sheba is in southwest Arabia, near Raamah, which is always mentioned together with it. Haran, Canneh, Eden (not to be confused with the garden in Genesis), and Ashur are in Mesopotamia. The name “Chilmad” is otherwise unknown and may be an inadvertent copyist’s error for the words “all of Media.” Tyre’s cargo list includes virtually every commodity that can be bought or sold, from slaves to horses, silver to saddle blankets, dyes to exotic spices. For Tyre’s involvement in the slave trade, see Joel 3:4–6.

No one in Ezekiel’s day can conceive of Tyre’s being defeated. However, her strength, wealth, and skill are no match for seas that obey the command of God.

**27:26 east wind.** The east wind often represents God’s judgment (see Ezek. 17:10; 19:12). Tyre’s fate will be a warning to all of the other nations that watch from the shore.

The third oracle addresses the prince of Tyre, who personifies the arrogance of the city. Her fate is his also. He lays claim to divinity and asserts that he sits on a throne in the heart of the chaotic and untamable sea. In the ancient Near East, the watery depths of the primeval ocean are a common symbol for the powers of chaos and death. Archaeologists have discovered more than one mythical creation account in which “the Sea” appears as a dragon or sea monster to be killed by the gods. Yet in reality, the prince of Tyre is only a man.

See note on 14:14. One aspect of the prince’s claim to divine status is his wisdom and ability to understand secrets, abilities like those of the prophet Daniel (cf. Dan. 8:26; 12:4). The king claims that his great wealth is due to this secret wisdom. As with the great ship in the previous oracle, though, his splendor is merely the precursor to his destruction. His death at the hands of the Babylonians will prove conclusively that he is indeed human and not divine. Instead of dwelling among the gods, he will be cast down to the pit, the home of the dead.

See note on 19:1–14. Laments often eulogize their subjects in glowing terms.

**king of Tyre.** Ethbaal rules Tyre at this time. The prophet describes the way God has favored Ethbaal by portraying the king as a primeval being, a figure like Adam, the crown and epitome of creation, living in the garden paradise that God made until, like Adam, wickedness is found in him (v. 15).

The garden of Eden was located on a mountain, which explains why a single water source could go out from there to water the four corners of the earth (Gen. 2:10–14). It also contained precious gemstones (Gen. 2:11, 12). In the Bible, encounters with God often take place on mountaintops (20:40; cf. Ex. 19:23; Deut. 33:2; Pss. 43:3; 48:1; 87:1; 99:9; Is. 27:13; 56:7; 57:13; 66:20). The temple was built on a mountain and was decorated with floral motifs (40:16–37; 41:18–20, 25–27; cf. 1 Kin. 6:29, 32, 35; 7:18, 20, 22, 36, 42; 2 Chr. 3:5).

**28:14 an anointed guardian cherub.** The garden of Eden was protected by cherubim, heavenly beings that guard the sanctity of the Lord’s holy things (Gen. 3:24; Ezek. 10). The king of Tyre is compared to these angelic creatures, who are higher and more holy than Adam himself. Some take the prophet to be comparing the king of Tyre to Satan, a glorious being who fell from grace (1 Tim. 3:6).

**stones of fire.** Possibly an obscure reference to a hedge of sparkling gemstones surrounding the garden of Eden. The jewels listed in this passage include nine of the twelve gemstones found on the high priest’s breastplate in Ex. 28.

verse_quote: I cast you as a profane thing.
note: This exalted (and perhaps sarcastic) description of the king of Tyre’s greatness prepares for the depth of his coming fall. Like Adam, he will be banished from the mountain of God, condemned to die for his rebellion against God.

Sidon is commonly paired with her trading partner Tyre, twenty-five miles (40 km) south on the Mediterranean coast. No specific charges are leveled against her; she is presumably guilty of the same offenses as her larger neighbor.

Not only willIsrael know the Lord’s power through His destruction of her enemies, but she will also experience God’s bringing her back to her land. Israel will then flourish since the nations that have been her adversaries will have been eliminated. With peace restored, she will undertake long-term projects such as building houses and planting vineyards (cf. Is. 65:21).

The six oracles against foreign nations in chs. 25–28 were directed largely against lesser states and the immediate neighbors of Israel. However, these four chapters are directed against Egypt, one of the great empires of the ancient world. This seventh oracle itself is made up of seven prophecies against Egypt, and all of them are dated (29:1, 17; 30:20; 31:1; 32:1, 17) except the prophecy beginning in 30:1.

**29:1 tenth year.** In 587 B.C., as Nebuchadnezzar is beginning to lay siege to Jerusalem.

Egypt is likened to a sea monster (vv. 3–5). The term used can designate both the abundant crocodiles of the Nile and the sea monster that represents chaos in the mythology of the ancient Near East. The Bible calls this mythological creature “dragon,” “Leviathan,” or “Rahab” (32:2; cf. Job 3:8; 7:12; 9:13 note; 41:1; Pss. 74:13, 14; 89:10; Is. 27:1; 30:7; 51:9; Rev. 12:15; 20:2). “Rahab” is also used as a poetic designation of Egypt (Ps. 87:4; Is. 30:7). In the mythology of the cultures surrounding Israel, this sea monster is a god who rivals other gods, but in the Bible it is demythologized as simply another creature living in submission to Yahweh’s command (see Gen. 1:21). In this oracle, the mythical overtones blend with the metaphor of Pharaoh as a fearsome crocodile resting in the Nile.

God will pluck this crocodile from the river as easily as anglers haul in fish, and He will leave it rotting on the shore. See note on 28:2. Like the images of Tyre as a mighty ship about to sink (ch. 27) and its king as the original man about to be cast from the garden (ch. 28), the image of Pharaoh as a giant crocodile paves the way for the introduction of God as the great hunter who will capture it.

The birds and animals are given to humankind as food (Gen. 1:30; 9:2, 3); the reversal of this relationship is a proverbial curse (32:4; cf. Deut. 28:26; Ps. 79:2; Jer. 7:33; 15:3; 16:4; 19:7; 34:20).

Ezekiel’s description of Egypt as a splintered reed recalls the Assyrian field commander’s similar comments to Hezekiah (2 Kin. 18:21). As with the other nations, Egypt’s sin has specific reference to its relationship with Israel and Judah. Egypt promised to support Judah in her rebellion against Babylon but proves unreliable. Though God’s people are guilty of trusting in Egypt and not in the Lord, Egypt is also guilty of soliciting and encouraging their disobedience., 7

The entire land of Egypt will be destroyed, from north to south (see also 30:6). Migdol is in northern Egypt, a site on the route of the exodus (Ex. 14:2; Num. 33:7; Jer. 44:1; 46:14). Syene is in southern Egypt at the first cataract on the Nile. It is the terminal point for deep-water navigation of the Nile and represents Egypt’s southern frontier.

It is difficult to fix a definite historical period of forty years for an Egyptian exile. The number may be symbolic of an entire generation rather than intended as a definite period (cf. Judah’s forty years of exile in 4:6). Egypt’s exile will be like Judah’s: she will be scattered to distant lands and then brought home by the Lord. Yet whereas Judah will be fully restored, Egypt will remain a shadow of her former self, no longer a source of temptation to God’s people.
This oracle is delivered in April 571 B.C., sixteen years after the preceding oracle (29:1). It is the latest date mentioned in the book, later even than the vision in chs. 40–48.

Nebuchadnez­zar’s siege of Tyre lasted for thirteen years (26:7 note). The siege was long and expensive, and the rewards did not repay the effort. To compensate Nebuchadnezzar for his labors, the Lord will reward him with the spoils of Egypt.

A horn is a common symbol for political power in the Bible (Deut. 33:17; 1 Sam. 2:10; 2 Sam. 22:3; Pss. 18:2; 75:4, 5, 10; 89:24; 92:10; 112:9; 132:17; 148:14; Jer. 48:25; Dan. 7:7, 8, 20, 21; Zech. 1:18–21; Rev. 17:12). This oracle against Egypt ends by finding hope for Israel (cf. 28:24–26). Even in the oracles against the nations, the primary focus always remains on God’s relationship with His own people.

**open your lips.** See notes on 24:27 and 33:22.

This is the only one of Ezekiel’s oracles against Egypt that is not dated. It may have been given between January and April 587 B.C. (29:1; 30:20). It repeats the content of the first oracle in the form of a lament.
Alongside Egypt, judgment will be poured out on all of her allies: Cush (Ethiopia), Put (part of Libya), Lud (Lydia), all Arabia, and Libya.
In the eastern Nile delta; also known as Tanis. This is near where the Israelites earlier worked as Egypt’s slaves.

Pelusium is a fortress on the Mediterranean coast, on Egypt’s northeastern frontier along with Tehaphnehes. On is an important religious center for Egypt located near the southern vertex of the Nile delta. Pi-beseth is mentioned only here in the Bible. It is in the eastern delta and served as a capital city during the twenty-third and twenty-second dynasties (950–725 B.C.).
Just as in the exodus plague, the light will be turned to darkness (Ex. 10:21–23).
April 586 B.C. Just before the fall of Jerusalem, ruling out any lingering hopes of help and deliverance from Egypt.

Pharaoh Hophra sends an army to assist Zedekiah, but it is repulsed (Jer. 37:1–10; cf. Ezek. 17:15–17; 29:6, 7). The “arm” is a figure for military power. The exiles living in Babylon and the people in Jerusalem have hoped that Pharaoh would defeat Babylon, but this prophecy denies them that hope. Instead, Babylon will break the arm of Pharaoh, leaving him unable to handle a sword, and useless as an ally for Israel. There is no hope of the arm healing or being bound up so that Pharaoh can return to the fray. The arm that remains whole will be broken, and the arm already broken will be broken once again, leaving Egypt totally defenseless, waiting for the final blow to fall. This fate is the result of the Lord strengthening the arms of Nebuchadnezzar.
June 586 B.C., a few months after the preceding oracle (30:20). Jerusalem is besieged and within weeks of being destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar.

The prophet uses the fate of Assyria as a warning to Egypt, for the once powerful Assyrian empire collapsed between 640 and 609 B.C. Some scholars think it unlikely that in an oracle against Egypt the primary focus should fall on Assyria (vv. 3–17). They suggest that a copyist’s error has altered one of the consonants in the text, and translate “Assyria” as “cypress” or “to what can I compare you,” a better parallel with the last clause in v. 2. With this correction, the whole passage is about Egypt.

**31:3 cedar.** Ezekiel has already used a similar symbol (ch. 17). Great trees can tower hundreds of feet and live for thousands of years; they provide an apt metaphor for kingdoms and dynasties (17:22–24). Much of the description of this tree resembles the supernatural tree in Nebuchadnezzar’s dream in Dan. 4:1–12, 19–27. The lavishness of Ezekiel’s description of this tree compares with the extravagance of his description of Tyre as a richly appointed merchant ship (27:3–11) and its ruler as the original man (28:11–19). The tree that represents Assyria is greater than all the great trees in the garden of God (that is, the garden of Eden). The great nations of the world live in its shade like birds and beasts that find shelter in the branches of a great tree.

Like Assyria, Egypt has forgotten that its greatness does not come from itself but is a gift of God. As with Tyre, such pride led to a great fall for Assyria as the divine lumberjack swung His ax of judgment. However high nations and empires set themselves, eventually they will all die and go down to the pit, the shadowy underworld that is the final resting place of the unworthy dead (26:15–21 note). The final state of the soul is not as clear in the OT as it is in the New, but it is nonetheless clear that those who die outside of fellowship with God face a bleak afterlife.

The scale of the cosmic tree, Assyria, sets the tone for the scale of the mourning at its fall.Lebanon, the home of cedar trees, was clothed in gloom, and the nations that lived in its shade were shocked at its demise. Just as Assyria was destroyed, so will Egypt come to complete ruin and destruction.
March 585 B.C., two months after the exiles have received news of the destruction of Jerusalem (33:21).

In the pagan mythology of the ancient Near East, the orderly universe emerges from chaos after a titanic battle between a god and a great sea monster or dragon called “Sea.” After the battle, parts of the universe are created from the carcass of the dead monster. Ezekiel refers to this myth in several places (28:2 note; 29:3–5). Here Ezekiel compares Pharaoh to a lion as well as to the great sea dragon. The word translated “dragon” also denotes a crocodile (29:3 note). The pharaohs in this era use both images, the lion and the crocodile, to describe themselves. Yet both crocodile and lion can be hunted and killed, as will happen to Pharaoh.

The language of this section is similar to that used to describe the day of the Lord in Is. 13:10; Joel 2:30, 31; 3:15; Amos 8:9. See note on 7:7. The appearance of God as the Divine Warrior is accompanied by convulsions in the created order. The universe dissolves into the chaos that existed before creation, when the heavens were dark (38:18–23 note). The huge corpse of the dead monster covers the earth and fills the valleys. Here the extravagant imagery is not meant literally but is used metaphorically to underscore the scale of the death of Pharaoh.

God will subdue the crocodile Egypt by bringing the armies of Babylon against her. The “sword of the king of Babylon” is in effect the sword of the Lord (ch. 21; 30:25). The destruction will be even greater than the first Passover, when only the firstborn humans and animals died (Ex. 12:29). In this case, all of the people and animals will die.
In his time of strength, the great crocodile thrashes around in the stream, stirring up mud. After his demise, the river will once again run smoothly and peacefully.
Probably the spring of 585 B.C.

The prophet has already described the descent of Egypt into the underworld (see 31:17, 18). There the proud empire became just one more among the many powerful states that preceded her (Assyria, v. 22; Elam, v. 24; Meshech and Tubal, v. 26; Edom, v. 29; Sidon and “the princes of the north,” v. 30). The underworld (“Sheol” or “the grave”) is commonly portrayed in the OT as a vast burial chamber where the dead have a shadowy and joyless existence. See note on Is. 14:9–11; also Gen. 37:35; Job 3:17–19; 7:9; 10:20–22; 17:13–16; Pss. 88:5, 11; 115:17; Prov. 1:12; 9:18; Eccl. 9:10; Is. 5:14; 38:18; Hab. 2:5.

**the uncircumcised.** The term is repeated ten times in vv. 19–32. The focus is not on the lack of the physical procedure but its spiritual significance. Those not initiated into the covenant community do not enjoy the Lord’s protection and eternal provision.
See note on 27:13.

This chapter marks the beginning of the second part of the book of Ezekiel. The first part of the book is primarily about Jerusalem in the past and present; the second part focuses on the future of the people of God.

**33:1–9** This part of the book begins by reiterating Ezekiel’s call to be a watchman (cf. 3:16–21). A watchman is appointed as a lookout for the community. In ch. 3, the focus was on Ezekiel’s responsibility as a watchman to declare the message faithfully. Here, Ezekiel is to tell the people that he is their watchman, shifting the focus onto their responsibility to hear the watchman’s warning. Even now that Jerusalem has fallen, they can still find life if they respond to the news with repentance.

Now that the prophet’s message of Jerusalem’s destruction has been vindicated, the people face the temptation to despair. They need to be reminded of the good news that the Lord does not take pleasure in destroying the wicked and is always ready to redeem those who repent and turn to Him. However, those who continue in their sins will surely be destroyed.

January 585 B.C. According to 2 Kin. 25:8–10, Jerusalem is destroyed by fire in the fifth month of the eleventh year of Jehoiachin’s rule. It is unlikely that it has taken more than a year and a half for the news to travel a distance that Ezra covers in four months (Ezra 7:9). Rather, with the exception of 24:1, Ezekiel is using a different system of reckoning years according to the years of his exile rather than the years of the king’s reign.

The prophet has been largely silent for a sustained period; see notes on 3:26 and 24:27. Now that the news of Jerusalem’s destruction has reached the exiles, his mouth is opened. The turning point in the prophet’s own life mirrors the turning point in the prospects of his people. As Ezekiel addresses (1) those who have remained in Judah after the destruction of the city (vv. 23–29) and (2) his fellow exiles (vv. 30–33), he recognizes that neither group has really changed. Those who have remained in Judah claim to be the sole remaining heirs of the promise to Abraham. Yet their behavior proves that they are not really Abraham’s offspring. Those whose lives completely deny Abraham’s faith cannot inherit the land promised to Abraham. Instead, they will inherit the curses of the Mosaic covenant: the sword, wild animals, and disease (v. 27; see Lev. 26:22–25).
This practice is forbidden in Gen. 9:4; Lev. 7:26, 27; 17:10; Deut. 12:16, 23.

The situation is little better among Ezekiel’s fellow exiles than it is in Judah. Now that events have confirmed the truth of his words, Ezekiel is no longer ignored and ridiculed but has become a popular form of entertainment. Yet the people still do not listen to the content of his messages so as to repent and obey (v. 11).

A flock of sheep is a common image in the Bible for God’s people, with the king as the undershepherd and God as the Great Shepherd (Ps. 23). Yet Israel’s shepherds (her kings) failed to protect their flock. Instead of taking care of the sheep that were weak, injured, or ill they fed themselves at the flock’s expense. They ruled the sheep with force and harshness (v.4), a phrase that recalls the abusive treatment that Israel faced at the hands of the Egyptians (Ex. 1:13, 14). As a result of their neglect and cruelty, the Lord’s flock has been scattered over the face of the earth.

Having set aside the unfaithful undershepherds, God Himself takes the role of shepherd (Luke 15:3–7), rescuing His flock from their grip. He will search for those who have been scattered and bring them safely home to the mountains of Israel, the center of the land God promised to Abraham. As in Ps. 23, the Lord will cause His flock to lie down on good grazing land and on rich pasture. He will bind up the injured and strengthen the weak.

verse_quote: a day of clouds and thick darkness.
note: This language is ordinarily associated with the day of the Lord (7:7 note; cf. Is. 60:2; Jer. 13:16; 23:12; Joel 2:1, 2; Amos 5:18–20; Zeph. 1:15).

God’s judgment is not confined to the shepherds, but will include the more powerful among the livestock. Some of the animals in the herd have been bullying others; these probably represent members of the upper classes of Jerusalem society who have oppressed the poor. There is a similar situation in the restoration community (Neh. 5).

This promise of restoration (vv. 6, 10–16) looks forward to the messianic kingdom. God’s Servant, one like David, the king after God’s own heart (1 Sam. 13:14), will rule in peace, righteousness, and prosperity exceeding that known during the rule of the historical David. No descendant of David in the restoration period fulfills Ezekiel’s prophetic description of Israel’s future king. The NT identifies Jesus as the Good Shepherd (John 10:11–14). He is the fulfillment of the promise to David in 2 Sam. 7 that one of his offspring will reign on his throne forever.
See note on 37:24.

This is not a covenant entirely new and different from the one made at Mount Sinai (cf. Rom. 8:3, 4). Rather, it is a covenant that actually achieves what the law promised at Mount Sinai but could never deliver because of Israel’s sin. In place of the covenant curse that Israel earned through their disobedience, the Lord will give His people covenant blessings, including safety, agricultural bounty in the land, and a restored relationship to the Lord (see Lev. 26:4–13).

**34:25 banish wild beasts.** Wild animals are a covenant curse for disobedience (Lev. 26:6; Deut. 33:20; 1 Kin. 13:24–28; 20:36; 2 Kin. 2:24; 17:25, 26;)., 26

See note on 6:7.

**with them ... my people.** The essence of God’s covenant with Israel is that the Lord will be their God, and they would be His people (11:20; 36:28; cf. Ex. 6:7; Lev. 26:12; Deut. 7:6; 14:2; 27:9; 29:13; Ps. 50:7; Is. 51:22; Jer. 7:23; 11:4; 30:22; Joel 2:27).

Edom is located along the margin of arable land southeast of the Dead Sea; Seir is the chief mountain range in the country. Mount Seir is used as a synonym for Edom (v. 15; Gen. 32:3; 36:8, 9; Deut. 2:8; Judg. 5:4; 2 Chr. 25:14). This oracle of judgment against Mount Seir forms a contrasting backdrop that showcases the Lord’s grace in restoring the mountains of Israel in ch. 36 (cf. Mal. 1:2–5).

The Edomites, descendants of Esau, helped King Nebuchadnezzar in his assault on Jerusalem, cutting off fugitives and handing them back to the Babylonians (Obad. 10–14; Mal. 1:2–5). This attitude was motivated both by a desire to take over their territory and by the ancient enmity against the descendants of Esau’s brother, Jacob (cf. Gen. 27). Because of that enmity, the Lord will judge Edom and bring its land to perpetual destruction.

Israel and Judah.

**we will take possession of them.** Cf. Deut. 2:2–6, a passage forbidding Israel to take the territory of Edom because God gave it to the descendants of Esau.

The prophecy of judgment directed against Mount Seir (ch. 35) is followed by a prophecy of restoration directed to the mountains of Israel. This reverses the devastation threatened for these same mountains in ch. 6, while the fate of Edom represents the fate of all of the enemies of Israel who have taunted her and possessed her land.
This phrase refers to the land God promised Israel, or if taken strictly, to the heights of Zion (17:23; 34:14; Deut. 32:13; Pss. 48:2; 78:69; Is. 58:14; Jer. 31:12).

Israel will prosper and be more populous than she was before the recent disaster (vv. 11, 12; cf. Zech. 2:4). The prophets often describe God’s future blessing on the land in terms of a multitude of children, when the covenant curses of barrenness and miscarriage are removed (37:25; Is. 49:20; 54:1; 59:21; Jer. 30:20; 31:17; Zech. 8:5).
Israel’s shame will be taken away and replaced by shame for her enemies.

In the past, Israel’s sin polluted their land, making it unfit for divine habitation in the same way that menstrual cloths were made unclean by contact with a woman’s monthly flow of blood. There was nothing sinful about this natural process, however, any loss of bodily life fluids, such as blood or semen, defiled people by distancing them from the realm of life. See note on 18:6.

When God judged His people for their sin and cast them out of their land, shame came upon His name, as the nations concluded that the Lord was unable to keep His people safe in their own land. Concern for the honor of His holy name led the Lord to scatter them, but the same concern for His name will also lead him eventually to re-gather the remnant of His people.

The sprinkling or pouring of water refers to the ritual purifications for removing religious defilement (Ex. 30:17–21; Lev. 14:52; Num. 19:17–19). It is also used as a symbol for the gift of God’s Spirit in the anointing of kings and priests and in the prophetic call (Joel 2:28, 29). The outpouring of God’s Spirit is a sign of the messianic age (37:14; 39:29; cf. Is. 42:1; 44:3; 59:21). This rich symbolism attaches to baptism in the NT. The language of vv. 25–27 is closely paralleled in Ps. 51:7–11.

See 11:19 and note on 18:31. The heart and the spirit are the location of the thoughts and the will that underlie actions. Israel’s transformation will not just be external but internal as well. Instead of a heart of stone, unable to respond to God with love and obedience, God will provide a new heart and a new spirit. Note that these changes come as the result of divine initiative and not human effort. Jeremiah describes the new covenant in the same way (Jer. 31:33 note; cf. Prov. 3:3; 7:3; Rom. 2:15, 29; 2 Cor. 3:3).

The new spirit will be the Spirit of God transforming those in whom He dwells and enabling them to obey the law of God. This is a work as glorious as the Spirit’s original work in creation. Cf. Gen. 1:2; Ezek. 37:1–10; Rom. 7:6; 8:2–17; Gal. 5:16–18, 22; 1 John 3:24.

Israel as a nation is God’s garden; see notes on 28:13, 14; 40:16; 47:1, 2. Yet this garden will be enhanced with cities overflowing with people like Jerusalem during the three great annual pilgrim festivals. The greatest blessing of all is the Lord’s willingness to hear Israel’s requests, unlike the former days when He would not let them inquire of Him (14:1–3; 20:1–3).

The OT does not present a complete doctrine of resurrection; this awaited the coming of Christ (Job 14:14; 19:25, 26; Dan. 12:2; cf. 1 Kin. 17:17–24; 2 Kin. 4:8–37; 13:21). Ezekiel’s vision is not about a general resurrection at the end of time; the question posed to him is not, “Can dry bones in general be brought back to life?” but rather, “Can these specific dry bones live?” The vision gives a specific and immediate hope to the exiles longing to be restored to their own country (37:14). Of course, the same God who raises these dry bones also brought back Jesus Christ from the dead as the firstfruits of the resurrection (1 Cor. 15:20), so the hope of this passage also has a wider application to all believers.

**37:1 Spirit.** The words “breath,” “Spirit,” and “wind” in this passage represent the same Hb. word, adjusted by translations to the requirements of context (vv. 1, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 14).

**valley.** This is the same term used in 3:22 (see note). It is also the same word used to describe the location of the Tower of Babel in Gen. 11:2. It is thus the opposite of the “very high mountain” where Ezekiel sees his vision in Ezek. 40:2.

Ezekiel sees not merely an assortment of recently deceased corpses but an enormous field of destruction, covered with dried-up and dismembered skeletons. For Ezekiel, The answer to the Lord’s question whether these bones can live must seem to be an obvious “No.” Yet the prophet cautiously turns the question back to the Lord, not presuming to be able to read His purposes. Obviously, the Lord has the power to do whatever He wants; the real question is whether it is His will to raise these dry bones.
At creation, God spoke and new life was created (Gen. 1). Ezekiel’s words are similarly efficacious in this vision, for they are also God’s words.

At first, the recreated bodies are lifeless, lacking spirit/breath. Like the creation of Adam in Gen. 2:7, the recreated Israel is first formed by God and then given life by the Spirit/breath of God. After the Spirit comes into the bodies, they stand on their feet like a mighty army, ready to serve. This recalls Ezekiel’s own calling; when the prophet fell prostrate in the presence of God’s glory, the Spirit entered him and brought him to his feet (1:28; 2:2; 3:22–24). Ezekiel is thus himself the firstfruits of the promised regeneration of God’s people., 10

The vision began with exposed and unburied bones (v. 2), but now broadens to include the opening of graves. The exiles feel themselves to be dead and buried, as helpless and hopeless as the field of dry bones. The vision confirms their utter helplessness, but it also points them to the One who not only has the power to give them a new hope but whose will it is that they should live again.
Israel’s restoration will be God’s own testimony to His power and rule.

The prophet performs another sign-act (4:1–3 note). Two sticks, one bearing the name of the southern kingdom Judah and the other bearing the name of the northern kingdom Ephraim (Israel), are held end-to-end in one of the prophet’s hands so that they appear to be joined.

The prophet interprets his symbolic actions (vv. 16, 17). Joseph’s two sons were Ephraim and Manasseh; these two tribes were the central part of the northern kingdom, so much so that the northern kingdom (Israel) is sometimes designated simply as “Ephraim” (2 Chr. 25:7, 10; Is. 7:2, 9, 17; 11:13; 17:3; Jer. 31:20; Hos. 4:17; 6:4; 8:9; 9:8; 10:6; Zech. 9:13). It fell to the Assyrians almost a century and a half before the exile of Judah, and the Israelites were dispersed among other nations and assimilated to them. This passage looks back to the united monarchy under David and Solomon, and forward to a future ideal restoration (33:24; Jer. 3:18; 23:5, 6; Hos. 1:11; Amos 9:11). The main point is not merely that Israel and Judah will be reunited, but that this is something the Lord Himself will do.

Ezekiel is reluctant to use the word “king” in reference to any of the historical rulers of Jerusalem, preferring instead to call them “prince” (v. 25; 12:10, 12; 19:1; 21:12, 25; 22:6; 34:24). Here, however, he describes the future Davidic ruler as “king” (v. 22, 24), because he is the one who unites the two separate kingdoms into one. The NT reveals that this shepherd-king is Jesus (34:2–10, 23 and notes), who reigns over the renewed people of God forever (v. 25; 34:31; John 10:11, 14; Matt. 2:2; Acts 5:31). The church—in which Jews, Samaritans, and Gentiles are united as a single people under one King, Jesus—is thus the fulfillment of this vision.

The repetition of “forever” (vv. 25, 26, 28) indicates that the reunification in view is eschatological, that is, an event to occur in the last days. The reunited people will also be a renewed people, cleansed from their idols and therefore able to dwell in God’s presence.

See 34:25 and note.

**everlasting covenant.** This eternal covenant took effect through the offering of Christ’s blood (Heb. 13:20).
See note on 34:30.

verse_quote: sanctuary is in their midst forevermore.
note: The renewed people are promised a new sanctuary in which God will once again dwell in their midst. After the description of the last battle in chs. 38; 39, Ezekiel will return to this theme to describe the renewed temple and land (chs. 40–48). More than six hundred years after Ezekiel, John has a similar vision (Rev. 21), but of a city that no longer needs a temple building because Christ is its center and sanctuary (Rev. 21:22).

Before his description of the future temple and land, the prophet first describes the assault and defeat of its foes (ch. 38), followed by their removal (ch. 39). Gog, the prince of Magog (v. 2 note), sums up the constant opposition to the kingdom and people of God. God comes as the Divine Warrior in a cataclysmic battle, fighting for His people and visiting an apocalyptic defeat on His foes, preparing the way for the vision of the renewed temple and land (chs. 40–48). If even the last enemy, Gog, cannot separate the Lord from His people, surely nothing in all creation can (Rom. 8:35–39).

The identity of Gog is uncertain. He is often identified with Gyges, the king of Lydia, a land in Anatolia (modern-day Turkey). In Akkadian texts from the seventh century, Gyges is known as an Assyrian vassal; later legend credits him with the invention of coinage. This identification is by no means certain, however, as the biblical character transcends normal historical categories and takes on tremendously fearsome proportions.

**Magog.** This land ruled by Gog is also otherwise unknown from extant geographical lists or citations in ancient literature; it may mean no more than “land of Gog.”

**Meshech and Tubal.** Though the identification of Gog and Magog remain uncertain, the identification of Meshech and Tubal is not in doubt (27:13 note). From the ancient historians Herodotus and Josephus, as well as Assyrian documents from the twelfth to the eighth centuries B.C., they are known to be tribes from central and eastern Anatolia (modern Turkey). Considerable misunderstanding has resulted from misguided speculation regarding these geographical terms. Some have identified these locations with other sites known from contemporary geography and have made them part of conjectures about later political events. Meshech and Tubal are sometimes said to be Moscow and Tobolsk, two Russian cities far distant from the region Ezekiel mentions. The Hebrew word translated “prince” (v. 2) is _rosh,_ and some have said that this means “Russia.” Even if this word is a geographical name and not to be translated “prince,” it is not “Russia.” The name “Russia” was brought into the region north of Kiev by the Vikings during the Middle Ages, and was not in use in Ezekiel’s time. The identification of _rosh_ with Russia was first made in the nineteenth century, around the time of the Crimean War, during a period when Russian expansionism threatened Europe.

In describing the threats to Israel’s existence, the Bible commonly refers to foes coming from the north (Is. 41:25; Jer. 1:13–15; 4:6; 6:22; 10:22; 13:20; 15:12; 25:9, 26; 46:10, 20, 24; 50:3, 9, 41; Ezek. 26:7; 38:6, 15; 39:2; Dan. 11; Zech. 2:6; 6:6–8; cf. Is. 5:26–29; 13:1–13; Hab. 1:5–11; Nah. 2:2–10; 3:1–3). References to these northern foes before the Babylonian exile in the sixth century B.C. usually point to Assyria, Babylon, and Persia, Israel’s traditional enemies. During and after the Babylonian exile, the foes from the north take on a more symbolic and apocalyptic coloring. In his description of conflict at the end of time, Ezekiel mentions tribes on the fringes of kingdoms to the north as an embodiment of the foes from the north that already figure in Israel’s eschatology (their understanding of the last days). Rather than add to speculation about future history, modern readers should understand that Ezekiel himself uses these nations as symbolic references to all powers arrayed against God’s people (cf. Rev. 19; 20). Ezekiel contains many oracles against foreign nations (chs. 29–32), but there is none specifically against Babylon, where he and the exiles are held in captivity. Some have suggested that Magog, Meshech, and Tubal are veiled references to Babylon, the immediate enemy. Gog and Magog recur in John’s apocalyptic description of future conflict between good and evil (Rev. 20:8).
See note on Is. 18:1.

Probably a group from the area north of the Black Sea, known to the Assyrians as the Gimirrai and to the Greeks as the Cimmerians. Gog leads a coalition of seven nations from the south and the north. The picture is of a total mobilization against the people of God. Yet even this act of cosmic rebellion is completely under God’s sovereign control; He brings these nations with hooks in their jaws, as one might direct the steps of a captured crocodile. Compare the divine summons to war in Joel 3:9–11.

**Beth-togarmah.** See note on 27:14.
An innumerable foe assembles (Jer. 4:13; Joel 2:2). The imagery of a thunderstorm recalls the threatening picture painted in the opening vision. Gog masks his appearance like God, coming in a storm.

verse_quote: you will devise an evil scheme.
note: Even though God brings the unholy alliance to accomplish His holy purposes, they are not forced to obey against their will. God is sovereign even over the thoughts that fill the minds of His adversaries. Gog comes for one purpose, but God has another purpose for him, as will become apparent in ch. 39.

The southwestern corner of the Arabian Peninsula (modern-day Yemen). The Sabeans are famous for trading (27:22, 23; 1 Kin. 10:1, 2; Job 6:19; Joel 3:8).

**Dedan.** A territory in southern Edom (25:13; 27:20; cf. Jer. 25:23; 49:8). The merchant nations of the world (see 27:20, 22) line up for their share of the anticipated plunder from this unequal contest.

Gog is not the one mentioned in earlier prophecies describing a foe from the north (v. 2 note). Those prophecies were completely fulfilled by Nebuchadnezzar’s destruction of Jerusalem. Instead of coming to be an agent of divine wrath against Israel, Gog will himself be destroyed by that same wrath.

God Himself will be Israel’s defender. In passages describing the appearance of God as the Divine Warrior, the prophets commonly speak of a corresponding convulsion in the created order; creation dissolves into primeval chaos (32:6–8 note; Is. 13:13; 24:18–20; Jer. 4:23–26; Joel 2:10, 30, 31; Hag. 2:6, 7, 21; cf. Judg. 5:4; Pss. 18:8; 46:3; 77:16–19). The Divine Warrior will bring upon their enemies the same covenant curses that earlier He brought against Judah.

verse_quote: I will give you to birds of prey.
note: Like a new Goliath, Gog’s fearsomeness is the prelude to his fall. He will be helpless before the living God, his body left exposed for the birds of the air and the beasts of the field.

verse_quote: I will not let my holy name be profaned.
note: Just as the Lord once made His holiness known through acts of judgment (36:21), so now He will make it known through His acts of salvation for His people.

The prophet uses a vivid image to describe how large the enemy army will be and how total its defeat: the Israelites will gather the weapons of the vanquished and have sufficient firewood to last for seven years (Ps. 46:9). Ironically, six different kinds of wooden weapons are the only items to survive the fire from heaven. Collecting this abandoned weaponry is Israel’s only contribution to the battle; all they have to do is watch the Lord in action.
Gog’s hordes will be buried on the borders of Israel, near the Dead Sea. After seven months of work, burial details will still be searching for bodies (vv. 14, 15).
Contact with a corpse renders one ceremonially unclean (Lev. 11:24–28, 39; 22:4), so the land will require cleansing by burying all of the dead bodies.

verse_quote: he shall set up a sign by it.
note:
Gog comes with all his hordes expecting God’s people to be easy prey. Instead of delivering Zion into his hands, God will instead give him a grave marker (Hb. _ziun_, an obvious play on words). Gog comes for a city, but he finds a grave instead (cf. Rev. 20:10).

**Hamon-gog.** The valley will be named “Valley of the Hordes of Gog.” This valley filled with the corpses of Gog’s army is a reversal of the vision in 37:1–10, wherein a valley of dead bones became an army.

See note on 29:5. Usually sacrifice means that animals become food. Here the image is reversed: the human enemies are sacrificed and the animals eat. By such a reversal of the created order (Gen. 1:30; 9:2, 3), the prophet shows the universe dissolving into chaos under God’s judgment (38:18–23 note). The same image is used in Rev. 19:17, 18 (Is. 34:6, 7; Jer. 46:10; Zeph. 1:7–9).
A region east of the Sea of Galilee known for its fine cattle (Deut. 32:14; Ps. 22:12; Amos 4:1).
These parts of a sacrificial animal are ordinarily offered to God (44:15; Lev. 3:17).

This section makes clear the lesson that Ezekiel’s hearers are to take away from this vision: God demonstrates His glory in all of history through the judgment and restoration of His people. The Babylonian exile does not show that God has failed in His promises—to the contrary, it demonstrates to Israel and to the nations alike that the Lord’s sovereignty is universal. Though God has afflicted His people, He has not abandoned them. He will bring them home (vv. 25–29), and He will transform them by His Spirit so that a similar judgment will not be necessary thereafter (36:26 note; 11:19; 18:31; 37:14; Joel 2:28). After describing how God will crush His enemies (chs. 38; 39), the prophet turns to a description of the glorious restoration of the people of God (chs. 40–48). If even Gog cannot destroy God’s new Israel, what enemy can ever separate them from His love (Rom. 8:31–39)?

Ezekiel’s vision of the restored temple combines many strands of biblical tradition. Ezekiel weaves together the familiar understanding of Jerusalem as the city where God has chosen to dwell with references to Mount Sinai and the garden of Eden. However, the city in Ezekiel’s vision is not called Jerusalem, and is geographically located significantly further to the north than Jerusalem. The old city of Jerusalem’s sins cannot simply be forgotten (see chs. 16; 23); her restoration includes a new name to match her new character (48:35).

An angel leads the prophet on a tour of the city, beginning at the gates to the outer court of the temple (40:6–27) and ending after several chapters with a division of land among the twelve tribes (47:13–48:35). Interpretations of these chapters vary widely. Some have seen in these passages a blueprint and building specifications for a temple that will be built in the future (43:10, 11). However, key details are omitted, such as the height of the buildings and the materials to be used, thereby precluding such an interpretation. Other elements of the prophetic vision also seem to go well beyond a literal understanding (e.g., 47:1–12). Other interpreters therefore understand Ezekiel’s temple vision as a largely symbolic description of the way God blesses His people in Christ, with the temple standing preeminently for the presence of God in the midst of His people. Through the use of a symbolic vision (40:2; Num. 12:6), the prophet describes through architecture, legislation, and geography a point in the future when the presence of God among His purified people will transcend anything Israel has experienced in history. Chapters 40–48 are thus the detailed unfolding of the promise given in 37:24–38.

**40:1 twenty-fifth year.** On the tenth day of the seventh month of a Jubilee year, which occurs every fifty years, a trumpet is sounded to proclaim the coming of liberty throughout the land (Lev. 25:8–13). Ezekiel receives his vision of a new future for his people approximately halfway between the exile and the restoration from exile.

Revelations from God in the OT often take place on mountaintops, notably Mount Sinai, where Moses received God’s law and the design for the tabernacle (Ex. 19–40). Moses also saw the Promised Land from another mountaintop, though he did not live to enter it (Deut. 34:1–4). So, too, Ezekiel receives legislation and a design for a sanctuary on top of a mountain even though he will not live to see it fulfilled.

An angelic guide conducts the prophet on his tour of the city (cf. Zech. 1:14). Like the heavenly creatures in Ezekiel’s opening vision, the angel’s appearance is like bronze.

**measuring reed.** See 2 Kin. 21:13; Amos 7:7, 8; Zech. 2:1, 2; Rev. 21:10, 15. Measuring is a key theme in Ezek. 40–48.
John receives similar instructions (Rev. 1:11). This vision holds a message for Ezekiel’s contemporaries, not just for those who would live at some distant time in the future.

The first thing the prophet sees is a tall and thick wall separating the area of the holy from the profane, a separation the priests failed to enact in 22:26. Access to the realm of the holy in the new temple is tightly regulated to prevent it from being profaned again.

**cubits.** There are at least two standard cubits, the short cubit of about 17.4 inches (44 cm), and the long cubit, used here, of about 20.4 inches (52 cm) (43:13; cf. 2 Chr. 3:3). The rod is about ten feet long (3 m).

With such high and thick walls, gates control access to the temple. The gate facing east is the most important of the gates and so is described first.

**going up its steps.** The temple is approached by steps to a raised platform that is the outer court. More steps lead to a higher platform that is the inner court (vv. 34, 37). A flight of stairs leads from there to the temple building (v. 49; 41:8). The higher the elevation and the closer to the inner sanctuary, the greater the degree of sanctity. The prophet’s tour starts from the outside and moves toward the center, which is reached at the end of ch. 41. He then returns outward, ending with the kitchens in the outer courtyard in 46:19–24.

These gateways resemble gates of the Solomonic period unearthed in excavations at Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer (1 Kin. 9:15), but they are significantly larger in size. The way through the center of the gate is flanked by three guardrooms on each side.

See also vv. 22, 31, 34, 37. The decoration in Israel’s ancient sanctuaries is mainly botanical; varieties of trees and plants decorate the sacred area (Ex. 25:34; 37:19; 1 Kin. 6:18, 29, 32, 35). In this respect the sanctuaries of Israel suggest the beauty of Eden and set before Israel the goal of again dwelling in God’s garden (28:13, 14 note).

Worshipers are admitted to the outer court, but only priests and Levites can enter the inner court. The text does not specify the exact dimensions or use of the thirty rooms on the perimeter of the outer court, which is another way of heightening the contrast between the less significant outer area of the temple and the crucial central holy space.

The northern and southern gates look the same as the eastern gate (vv. 5–16). There is no western gate because the area behind the Most Holy Place is blocked off to prevent access to the temple from the rear.

The inner court is separated from the outer court and is elevated by a further eight steps. It also has three substantial gateways (vv. 28–37). There is no mention of a wall, however. It may be that the elevation provides sufficient separation while still allowing a clear view of activities within the inner area, or mention of the wall may simply be omitted.

Animals offered for sacrifice are slaughtered in the gateways to the inner court (43:13–27). After the animals have been slaughtered, the parts are washed (cf. Lev. 1:9, 13; 2 Chr. 4:6) and hung on hooks (v. 43). The time spent on this detail highlights the radical focus of the new temple as a place of sacrifice for atonement, in contrast to Solomon’s temple, which was equally a place of sacrifice and a house of prayer (1 Kin. 8:28–30; Is. 56:7).

verse_quote: the sons of Zadok, who alone ... may come near.
note: See note on 44:15. Another important theme in these chapters is the restriction of access to God to those whom He has chosen and who are fit to enter the holy space.

The themes of sacrifice and restricted access come together in the description of the inner courtyard, which is a perfect square, like all holy spaces in the OT. The altar of sacrifice, where the Zadokite priests alone will offer the sacrifices, is at the geometric center of this court.

Like Solomon’s temple before it, the temple of Ezekiel’s vision has three rooms: a vestibule or portico (40:48, 49); an outer sanctuary (41:1, 2); and the inner sanctuary or Most Holy Place (41:3, 4). The temple building is set higher than the surrounding courtyard and reached by stairways leading to the portico (40:6 note). The increase in height represents increasing sanctity as one approaches the inner room. The temple building also has thick walls, but since access is already restricted, gates can be replaced by simple doors. Because the sanctuary is the most important space of the new temple, it is described in the most detail and with the most precise measurements. The sanctuary and its associated spaces make a second 100-cubit square, matching the inner courtyard.
The pillars presumably resemble Jachin and Boaz, the pillars that stood outside Solomon’s temple (1 Kin. 7:15–22).

Access to the Most Holy Place is restricted to the high priest on the Day of Atonement (Lev. 16; cf. Heb. 9:11–14). As a measure of the restrictive access in the new temple, the angel can enter this room, but Ezekiel cannot—even before the Lord’s glory returns to take up residence there (43:1–5).

The Most Holy Place in the tabernacle and the Most Holy Place in Solomon’s temple are also perfect cubes, equal in length, width, and height (cf. Rev. 21:16). In Ezekiel’s temple, the Most Holy Place is accessed by openings of increasing narrowness.

Rooms are built around the north, west, and south sides of the temple building. They are probably used to store equipment and the wealth of the temple (cf. 42:13; 1 Kin. 6:5–10). The second and third stories are offset so that each is a cubit wider than the level below. The building to the rear of the temple may simply protect it from unauthorized access.

The cherubim are like those described in Ezekiel’s earlier oracles of judgment (1:5–9 note). However, when carved in relief, they are depicted with two faces instead of four. These traditional images of the Lord’s heavenly bodyguards also adorned the tabernacle and Solomon’s temple (Ex. 26:1; 1 Kin. 6:29).
The table of the bread of the Presence is described as an altar only here, highlighting Ezekiel’s focus on the temple as a place of sacrifice.

These rooms should not be confused with those built on the perimeter of the temple building itself (41:5–12 note). These are along the north and south sides of the wall separating the inner and outer courts, and are used for activities that the priests had to perform on the way into and out of the inner court with its increased level of sanctity. These regulations represent a significant increase in the care taken to separate the holy from the profane when compared to the equivalent laws in Leviticus (see 42:20).

The outer wall separates the sacred precincts from the secular; see note on 40:7. By ending where he began, with the wall, Ezekiel focuses on this principle of separation.

**500.** Five hundred cubits is the sum of the lengths of the north outer gateway (50), part of the outer court (100), the north inner gateway (50), the inner court (100), the south inner gateway (50), part of the outer court (100), and the south outer gateway (50). Unlike the less-regular design of the tabernacle and Solomon’s temple, Ezekiel’s temple complex is itself square.

The prophet had an earlier vision of the glory of the Lord departing from the city (10:18–22; 11:22–24); now in his vision he witnesses its return. The glory comes from the east, the direction to which it had departed (11:23). Unlike its slow and halting departure, the return of the glory is sudden and rapid, accompanied by the characteristic roar of many waters (see 1:24), leading the prophet once again to fall on his face. The glory of the Lord filled the tabernacle and Solomon’s temple when they were dedicated (Ex. 40:34, 35; 1 Kin. 8:10, 11; 2 Chr. 5:13, 14; 7:1, 2; cf. Is. 60:1–3). See note on 11:22–24. The temple of the restoration period, built by Zerubbabel, is not built according to Ezekiel’s vision. It is a rebuilt version of Solomon’s temple, though lacking its earlier splendor (Ezra 3:12, 13; Hag. 2:3). Yet Haggai prophesies that the glory of Zerubbabel’s temple will exceed that of Solomon’s (Hag. 2:7–9), because God’s presence will be there. Ultimately, this is fulfilled in Christ and His temple, the church.

The Jerusalem temple is understood as the place where God had His throne, where He is enthroned in the Most Holy Place above the ark, which is His footstool (1 Sam. 4:4; 2 Sam. 6:2; 2 Kin. 19:15; 1 Chr. 13:6; Pss. 80:1; 99:1; 132:13, 14; Is. 6:1; 37:16). The significant part of the affirmation is that this temple will be the Lord’s throne forever; the sins of His people will never again drive Him away from His sanctuary.

**the dead bodies of their kings.** In the past, Israel’s kings defiled the temple both by their spiritual adultery and by placing memorial markers for dead kings in the grounds of the temple of the living God. In the future, the kings will be put in their proper place at a greater distance from the residence of the great King, God Himself.

The patterns for Israel’s past sanctuaries have come from God; likewise, the plans for the temple in Ezekiel’s vision are of divine origin. See note on 40:1–48:35. This vision is not intended to provide the blueprint for a building project; rather, it has a message for Ezekiel’s contemporaries. As they study the plan, they are to be convicted of their sins and ashamed of their iniquities. By permitting and restricting access to particular groups of people and raising the general standards of holiness throughout the sacred space, Ezekiel communicates the same message of the necessity of absolute holiness that he has proclaimed elsewhere in more direct form.

Ezekiel’s temple vision is the only body of ritual law in the Bible not from the mouth of Moses. Like Moses, Ezekiel receives this law on a high mountain (40:2; Ex. 25:9, 40). This law is not intended to replace the laws of Moses, with which it cannot be harmonized. Rather, it is another way of making the same fundamental points as Ezekiel’s visionary temple. Here, theology is described in the form of legislation.

See note on 40:5.

**altar.** The altar is built as a series of platforms, each smaller than the one below, similar to a step-pyramid or ziggurat. The ancient rabbis had many discussions about this altar since its construction contradicts the command that the altar should not have steps (Ex. 20:24–26). The steps ascend the east side to prevent any repetition of the sun worship in 8:16, where the people turned their backs on God. The importance of the sacrificial aspect of temple life is emphasized by the massive size of the altar and its location at the geometric center of the entire temple complex.
See Ex. 29:16; Lev. 4:6; 5:9. The new altar must be consecrated before it can be put into use (2 Chr. 7:8, 9). A similar procedure was followed when the altar of Solomon’s temple was consecrated.
See note on 44:15.
See Ex. 29:14; Lev. 4:12, 21; 8:17; 9:11; 16:27. The writer of Hebrews interprets these instructions as an aspect of Christ’s offering of Himself (Heb. 13:11–13).

The prophet has been in the inner court (43:5), but he is now taken to the eastern gate. That gate will remain closed because the glory of the Lord has entered the temple through it (v. 2; 43:4; cf. Ps. 24:7–10). That the gate is closed may also imply that the Lord will never leave the temple again (43:7, 9).

Since the gate is closed, the gateway becomes a room; in this room the prince will be allowed to eat his portion of sacrificial meals. In Ezekiel’s vision it represents the special relationship the promised king will maintain with the Lord. See note on 37:24.

While some portions of the OT emphasize restrictions on the participation of foreigners in Israel’s worship (Ex. 12:43; Lev. 22:25; Neh. 9:2; Jer. 51:51), other passages anticipate the participation of foreigners (47:22, 23; cf. 1 Kin. 8:41, 43; 2 Chr. 6:32, 33; Is. 56:3, 6–8; cf. Zech. 14:21; Eph. 2:12, 19). Similar restrictions on foreigners characterize other writings from the period after the Babylonian exile (Ezra 4:1–3; 10:10–44; Neh. 13:1–9; Hag. 2:14). The issue in this passage is not merely that these people are foreigners but that they are uncircumcised—that is, they have not become part of God’s people. Most likely, this refers to the practice of using foreign mercenaries to guard the temple (2 Kin. 11:14–19), a role that the Lord specifically assigns to the Levites (Num. 1:53). In the New Israel of the new covenant, the church, all such distinctions between Jew and Gentile have been removed, as Jews and Gentiles together become part of the one new people of God in Christ (Eph. 2:11–18; 3:6).

The tasks that have wrongly been delegated to uncircumcised foreigners will once again be performed by the Levites (Num. 1:50–53; 3:6, 8, 28–32; 1 Chr. 23:24–32; 2 Chr. 8:14, 15). Though the Levites were involved in the people’s sin of idolatry and therefore could not enter the inner court as the priests would, they yet retained an important role. The priesthood itself was restricted to the line of Zadok, who has persevered in faithfulness to God (v. 15; 40:45, 46). The reward for that past faithfulness is closer access to God’s presence, while those who were unfaithful are kept at a distance from the Lord.

Zadok served as high priest alongside Abiathar during the reign of David (2 Sam. 15:24–29; 20:25). Abiathar was dismissed because he supported Adonijah against Solomon (1 Kin. 1:7; 2:26), but Zadok supported Solomon and became the only high priest. The priesthood had earlier been restricted among the Levites to the descendants of Aaron (Ex. 28:1; Lev. 8:2–7; 9:1–24; Num. 20:25–28; 1 Chr. 6:48–53), and Ezekiel foresees a further restriction to one family from Aaron.

The corollary of increased access for the Zadokite priests is heightened responsibility in ritual holiness. Their behavior is far more strictly regulated than that of the people as a whole. They have to wear only linen rather than wool so that they will not be defiled by the emission of sweat. They cannot come into contact with the realm of the dead, whether by contact with a dead body or by observing ritual mourning practices (see Lev. 21:1–12). The priests are not to drink wine when on duty, since priestly mistakes can have fatal consequences (see Lev. 10:9). They can marry only a virgin or the widow of a priest so that there will be no question as to the priestly bloodline of any children of the marriage. Again, the prophet insists on a radical distinction between holy and the common, the unclean and the clean (v. 23).
For the judicial role of the priests, see 1 Chr. 26:29; 2 Chr. 19:8–11.

The rest of Israel will receive a share in the reallocated Promised Land (see 47:13–48:35), but the priests will receive no share of their own since the Lord is their inheritance. They are to be provided for through the regular offerings and sacrifices made at the temple.

verse_quote: eat of anything ... that has died of itself.
note: The prohibition against eating meat of an animal found dead is part of the priests’ radical separation from the realm of death.

The allocation of the land will be taken up in greater detail in ch. 47. The concern here is the sacred precincts, where the priests and Levites will live. Ezekiel describes a sacred area in the middle of the land, a square of 25,000 cubits (about 8 miles; 13 km) on a side, further subdivided into three strips of land (cf. Rev. 21:16). The northern zone (about 25 square miles; 65 square km) is set aside for the use of the Levites. The central zone contains the sanctuary and is set apart for the priests. The southern zone, about half the size of the other two, is given to the city itself. The area east and west of the eight-mile square is given to the prince, while the area north and south is to be divided among the other tribes. Interestingly, in Ezekiel’s vision the temple itself is outside the city proper, maintaining a buffer zone against the sacred being defiled by the entry of the profane. The key element in the restoration of the land is to maintain the purity necessary for the Lord to dwell in the midst of His people. It is also the Lord who distributes the land, not the princes.

The prince’s primary responsibility was to establish justice and righteousness among the people. The prince himself was assigned enough land to meet his own needs and to support the ministry of the temple without burdening the people. The measures he uses to collect the people’s tithes and offerings for the temple are to be just, instead of adjusting the scales to secure profit for himself. Apparently the use of false weights and balances was common prior to the exile (Lev. 19:35, 36; Deut. 25:13–16; Prov. 11:1; Amos 8:5; Mic. 6:10–12).

**45:10 ephah ... bath.** The ephah is a dry measure of about five gallons (19 L). The bath is a liquid measure of about six gallons (23 L).
Ten baths or ephahs make a homer, or about fifty gallons (190 L).
A shekel is about two-fifths of an ounce (11 g); a mina of sixty shekels is about a pound and a half (0.7 kg). The mina is normally fifty shekels.

Israel’s princes are also responsible to make offerings on behalf of the people (vv. 13–17). The people will give offerings in kind to the prince, who in turn provides them to the sanctuary (cf. 2 Chr. 30:24). See notes on 37:24; 44:3.

These regulations cover aspects of the ceremonial observances of New Year’s Day (vv. 18–20), Passover (vv. 21–24), and Tabernacles (v. 25) in the seventh month. This legislation represents dramatic modifications of earlier liturgical practice, replacing the three distinctive festivals of the Mosaic calendar with two festivals that are virtually identical. The central focus of both festivals is on purification from sin, a central theme in these chapters.
Compare the consecration of the altar in Ex. 29:35–37.
A liquid measure of about one gallon (3.6 L).

The prince will be allowed to enter as far as the inner threshold of the eastern gate into the inner courtyard on festival days; on other days he will enter and leave with the ordinary people (vv. 9, 10) unless he is making a freewill offering (v. 12). The prince has special privileges with reference to the eastern gate in the outer courtyard (44:1 note; 44:3 note), though nothing like the control over worship exercised by the kings before the Babylonian exile (e.g., 2 Kin. 16:10–12). From his vantage point at the threshold of the inner gate, the prince will have a full view of the inner courtyard and the great altar; but entry to the inner court is restricted to priests and Levites. In contrast, the ordinary people are to offer their worship outside the gateway to the inner court, separated from the inner court by eight steps and a corridor that is ninety feet long.
The specifications for this offering differ from the Sabbath offerings in Num. 28:9, where two lambs and no ram are required.
The first day of the month. The specifications again differ from earlier legislation (Num. 28:11).

verse_quote: the prince shall enter with them.
note: The prince accompanies the people as they pass through the temple, acting as their representative in worship.

Whereas most of the preceding regulations concern offerings on particular days of the OT liturgical calendar, God is to be worshiped every day in Israel (vv. 13–15). The provisions for these daily offerings differ from earlier practice (Num. 28:3–8; 2 Kin. 16:15; 1 Chr. 16:40; 2 Chr. 13:11; 31:3). The meal imagery of these sacrifices depicts the regular table fellowship and communion between the Lord and His people.

In redeeming Israel from Egypt and later Babylon, God removed them from the place of bondage but also secured for them an inheritance in their own land. The land was supposed to be inalienable (Lev. 25:14–17, 23, 24; 1 Kin. 21), representing the permanence of the redemption and inheritance that God provided (1 Pet. 1:4). These verses address the previously common temptation for the prince to acquire additional lands with which to provide for his children or to reward his loyal servants, thereby oppressing the ordinary people.
Most likely a reference to the Year of Jubilee (Lev. 25:8–17; 27:24; Is. 61:1, 2).

OT worship combines sacrifice and prayer with eating and social activity. These regulations specify the places where the Levites prepare offerings for the sacrificial meals that are eaten by worshipers. The tour of the temple ends where it began, at the outside of the outer court.

The courtyard of the tabernacle had a large basin or laver where the priests washed (Ex. 30:17–21). Solomon’s temple housed a much larger Sea (1 Kin. 7:23–26). This Sea was used for ritual washing (2 Chr. 4:6), but it also symbolized the primeval ocean, no longer a menacing symbol of chaos (28:2 note) but subjected by God to the service of His temple. In Ezekiel’s temple vision, these earlier basins are replaced by a life-giving river (Rev. 21:1; 22:1, 2). The tabernacle laver and the temple Sea stand south of the altar in the sanctuary courtyard; the river likewise originates from south of the altar. This passage should be compared with others that speak of a river in the city of God (Ps. 46:4) or describe the eruption of a stream in the city (Joel 3:18; Zech. 14:3–8). Since the temple in part symbolizes paradise, Ezekiel’s river recalls the rivers issuing from the garden of Eden (Gen. 2:10–14)., 2

The river brings life everywhere it goes, transforming Israel into a paradisiacal garden.
