It brings life to even the lifeless salt waters of the Dead Sea, recalling the transformation of the dry bones in ch. 37. What is more, this unearthly river grows dramatically from small beginnings to become a mighty torrent that is impossible to cross. The exiles are to notice this and remember that the work of God often begins in small ways but culminates in grandeur (Zech. 4:10; Matt. 13:31, 32). Jesus appealed to the images used in this passage to describe Himself. He told the Samaritan woman that He is the source of life-giving water (John 4:10–14). When the disciples were surprised that Jesus was talking with a Samaritan woman, He spoke to them of an unending harvest that had already begun (John 4:27–38), drawing on Ezekiel’s picture of trees bearing twelve crops a year. John also records Jesus’ saying that He is the source of streams of living water, adding the comment that Jesus was speaking of God’s Spirit (John 7:37–39).
From one side of the Dead Sea to the other. A mark of the new life in the sea is the abundance of fish where previously there were none.
The swamps and marshes will be left for salt. Salt is a useful commodity and under the old covenant is often used in covenant-making ceremonies because of its unchanging character.

In Ezekiel’s vision, the land will be divided equally among the twelve tribes. Since the tribe of Levi receives its territorial inheritance inside the sacred precincts of Jerusalem (45:1–8 note), the number twelve is maintained by substituting for Joseph the two sons of Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh (Gen. 48:1–6). Israel and Judah are now reunited into a single nation (see 37:15–28).
This is the land God promised to the patriarchs (Gen. 12:7; 15:18–21; 22:17; 28:4), and that was possessed during the reigns of David and Solomon (1 Kin. 8:65; 1 Chr. 13:5; 2 Chr. 9:26).

The boundaries detailed here (vv. 15–20) mention a number of sites that are not known, but they roughly correspond to other such lists of sites (Num. 34:1–12; 1 Kin. 8:65). The eastern and western borders are easy to identify: on the east, the boundary begins in the headwaters of the Jordan south of Damascus, down the Jordan River, and along the western shore of the Dead Sea; on the west, the border is the Mediterranean Sea. The northern and southern borders are more difficult to establish: in the north, the line begins near Tyre and proceeds east to a point north of the Sea of Galilee; in the south, it runs from a point below the Dead Sea to the Brook of Egypt (the Wadi el-Arish) on the Mediterranean coast. Strikingly absent is the Transjordan, the area east of the Jordan River. Although this is historically the home of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, it is not part of the original land promised to Moses.

In Ezekiel’s vision, the allotment of the land among the tribes is different from what it was before the exile. Each tribe is allotted a horizontal strip of land connecting with the eastern and western borders, aligned with the sacred east-west axis of the temple. The statuses of Jacob’s wives and of the individual tribes seem to be the determining factors in the arrangement of the tribes (cf. Num. 2, 3). The northernmost tribes (Dan, Asher, and Naphtali) are traditionally located in the north; the southernmost tribe (Gad, v. 27) is historically a northern tribe. These four tribes are the sons of Leah’s servant Zilpah and Rachel’s servant Bilhah (Gen. 30:3–8, 10–13); as such they are located at the outer extremities of the tribal allotments in Ezekiel’s vision.

Judah is the closest tribe north of the sacred area in the center of the land (vv. 8–22; 45:1–8). Judah is historically a southern tribe; by presenting the tribe of David as part of the northern tribes, Ezekiel may be saying in effect that the North will have a portion in David (cf. 2 Sam. 20:1; 1 Kin. 12:16; 2 Chr. 10:16). Judah is in the place of honor that normally belongs to the firstborn, Reuben. Reuben is located immediately north of Judah. Next are the two tribes of Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh, descendants of Jacob through the favored wife Rachel.

The nearest tribe south of the sacred area is Benjamin. Its favored place reflects the favored status of Rachel and balances the favored position of the Joseph tribes in the north. The remaining three southern tribes (Simeon, Issachar, and Zebulun) are the descendants of Leah. Historically, Issachar and Zebulun hold allotments in the north.

This description is an elaboration of 45:1–8. The length of the description of this single portion compared to the brief description of the portions for the tribes highlights its central importance. The holy strip is not in the geographical center of the land, since there are seven tribes to the north and five to the south. Nonetheless, the spiritual center of the land has moved considerably north of the old location in Jerusalem.
See note on 44:15.

The city has twelve gates named for the twelve tribes (cf. Rev. 21:12–14). The focus on the exits of the city underlines the theme of access that runs through these chapters. Since one gate is named after Levi, Ephraim and Manasseh are replaced by their father Joseph. Unusually, the three most important gates face north, rather than east, so that they can open toward the temple. The city is a visible symbol of unity for the twelve tribes, and presumably contains residents from each tribe.

The city that used to be known as Jerusalem now receives a new name to match its transformed status. From the beginning of the OT, God revealed His intention to be with His people. He walked and spoke with them in the garden of Eden and dwelled in sanctuaries built in their midst. The promise of a child named Immanuel points to a day when God would be “with us” (Is. 7:14 text note). The NT ends in much the same way as the book of Ezekiel ends. John, too, describes the city of God, and a time when God will live with human beings face-to-face (Rev. 21:3); he ends with the prayer, “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus” (Rev. 22:20).
